In probabilistic terms, the aforementioned infinitely divisible process is equal to the conditional cumulative hazard process associated with the exchangeable sequence of random variables with minimum (or maximum) infinitely divisible marginals. Our results provide an analytic umbrella which embeds the de Finetti subfamilies of many interesting classes of multivariate distributions, such as exogenous shock models, exponential and geometric laws with lack-of-memory property, min-stable multivariate exponential and extreme-value distributions, as well as reciprocal Archimedean copulas with completely monotone generator and Archimedean copulas with log-completely monotone generator.

A new calibration method for H-fs-TALIF is proposed, and the ratio of two-photon absorption cross-sections, $ sigma^{(2)}$, for atomic hydrogen (H) and krypton (Kr) is determined for the broadband emission of a femtosecond laser system. The estimated ratio of the two-photon absorption cross-sections for H and Kr is $ sigma^{(2)}$ for H and Kr $ sigma^{(2)}$(Kr)/$ sigma^{(2)}$(H) = $0.027 pm 20$%, which is nearly twenty times lower than values previously obtained with narrowband nanosecond lasers. This discrepancy highlights the need for independent calibration of TALIF measurements for a specific laser pulsewidth range.

Recovering images from optical interferometric observations is one of the major challenges in the field. Unlike the case of observations at radio wavelengths, in the optical the atmospheric turbulence changes the phases on a very short time scale, which results in corrupted phase measurements. In order to overcome these limitations, several groups developed image reconstruction techniques based only on squared visibility and closure phase information, which are unaffected by atmospheric turbulence. We present the results of two techniques used by our group, which employed coherently integrated data from the Navy Prototype Optical Interferometer. Based on these techniques we were able to recover complex visibilities for several sources and image them using standard radio imaging software. We describe these techniques, the corrections applied to the data, present the images of a few sources, and discuss the implications of these results.

We embed spherical Rindler space -- a geometry with a spherical hole in its center -- in asymptotically AdS spacetime and show that it carries a gravitational entropy proportional to the area of the hole. Spherical AdS-Rindler space is holographically dual to an ultraviolet sector of the boundary field theory given by restriction to a strip of finite duration in time. Because measurements have finite durations, local observers in the field theory can only access information about bounded spatial regions. We propose a notion of Residual Entropy that captures uncertainty about the state of a system left by the collection of local, finite-time observables. For two-dimensional conformal field theories we use holography and the strong subadditivity of entanglement to propose a formula for Residual Entropy and show that it precisely reproduces the areas of circular holes in AdS3. Extending the notion to field theories on strips with variable durations in time, we show more generally that Residual Entropy computes the areas of all closed, inhomogenous curves on a spatial slice of AdS3. We discuss the extension to higher dimensional field theories, the relation of Residual Entropy to entanglement between scales, and some implications for the emergence of space from the RG flow of entangled field theories.

In this paper, we find a family $SL^{n,m}$, in any arbitrary dimensions, of cohomologically rigid solvable Lie superalgebras with nilradical the model filiform Lie superalgebra $L^{n,m}$. Moreover, we exhibit a family of cohomologically rigid solvable Lie superalgebras with nilradical the model nilpotent Lie superalgebra of generic characteristic sequence. Both cases correspond to solvable Lie superalgebras of maximal dimension for a given nilradical. Contrariwise, we will show that the family of Lie superalgebras $SL^{n,m}$ can be deformed if defined over a field of odd characteristic.

Existences of vector-like quarks (VLQs) are predicted in many new physics scenarios beyond the Standard Model (SM). We study the possibility of detecting the vector-like bottom quark (VLQ-$B$) being the $SU(2)$ singlet with electric charge $-1/3$ at the Large Hadron Electron Collider (LHeC) in a model-independent framework. The decay properties and single production of VLQ-$B$ at the LHeC are explored. Three types of signatures are investigated. By carrying out a fast simulation for the signals and the corresponding backgrounds, the signal significances are obtained. Our numerical results show that detecting of VLQ-$B$ via the semileptonic channel is better than via the fully hadronic or leptonic channel.

The pharmacopeia used by physicians and lay people in medieval Europe has largely been dismissed as placebo or superstition. While we now recognise that some of the materia medica used by medieval physicians could have had useful biological properties, research in this area is limited by the labour-intensive process of searching and interpreting historical medical texts. Here, we demonstrate the potential power of turning medieval medical texts into contextualised electronic databases amenable to exploration by algorithm. We use established methodologies from network science to reveal statistically significant patterns in ingredient selection and usage in a key text, the fifteenth-century Lylye of Medicynes, focusing on remedies to treat symptoms of microbial infection. We discuss the potential that these patterns reflect rational medical decisions. In providing a worked example of data-driven textual analysis, we demonstrate the potential of this approach to encourage interdisciplinary collaboration and to shine a new light on the ethnopharmacology of historical medical texts.

Attosecond streaking of atomic photoemission holds the promise to provide unprecedented information on the release time of the photoelectron. We show that attosecond streaking phase shifts indeed contain timing (or spectral phase) information associated with the Eisenbud-Wigner-Smith time delay matrix of quantum scattering. However, this is only accessible if the influence of the streaking infrared (IR) field on the emission process is properly accounted for. The IR probe field can strongly modify the observed streaking phase shift. We show that the part of the phase shift ( time shift ) due to the interaction between the outgoing electron and the combined Coulomb and IR laser fields can be described classically. By contrast, the strong initial-state dependence of the streaking phase shift is only revealed through the solution of the time-dependent Schr  odinger equation in its full dimensionality. We find a time delay between the hydrogenic 2s and 2p initial states in He+ exceeding 20as for a wide range of IR intensities and XUV energies.

The radial drift and diffusion of dust particles in protoplanetary disks affect both the opacity and temperature of such disks as well as the location and timing of planetesimal formation. In this paper, we present results of numerical simulations of particle-gas dynamics in protoplanetary disks that include dust grains with various size distributions. We consider three scenarios in terms of particle size ranges, one where the Stokes number $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-1} - 10^0$, one where $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-4} - 10^{-1}$ and finally one where $ tau_{ rm{s}} = 10^{-3} - 10^{0}$. Moreover, we consider both discrete and continuous distributions in particle size. In accordance with previous works we find in our multi-species simulations that different particle sizes interact via the gas and as a result their dynamics changes compared to the single-species case. The larger species trigger the streaming instability and create turbulence that drives the diffusion of the solid materials. We measure the radial equilibrium velocity of the system and find that the radial drift velocity of the large particles is reduced in the multi-species simulations and that the small particle species move on average outwards. We also vary the steepness of the size distribution, such that the exponent of the solid number density distribution, $ rm{d} it{N}/ rm{d} it{a}  propto  it{a^{-q}}$, is either $q = 3$ or $q = 4$. We measure the scale height of the particles and observe that small grains are stirred up well above the sedimented midplane layer where the large particles reside. Our measured diffusion and drift parameters can be used in coagulation models for planet formation as well as to understand relative mixing of the components of primitive meteorites (matrix, chondrules and CAIs) prior to inclusion in their parent bodies.

We report the identification of LP 400-22 (WD 2234+222) as a very low-mass and high-velocity white dwarf. The ultraviolet GALEX and optical photometric colors and a spectral line analysis of LP 400-22 show this star to have an effective temperature of 11080+/-140 K and a surface gravity of log g = 6.32+/-0.08. Therefore, this is a helium core white dwarf with a mass of 0.17 M_solar. The tangential velocity of this white dwarf is 414+/-43 km/s, making it one of the fastest moving white dwarfs known. We discuss probable evolutionary scenarios for this remarkable object.

As in our previous work [1] we address the problem to determine the splitting of the normal bundle of rational curves. With apolarity theory we are able to characterize some particular subvarieties in some Hilbert scheme of rational curves, defined by the splitting type of the normal bundle and the restricted tangent bundle.

We describe two ground based observing campaigns aimed at building a grid of approximately 200 spectrophotometric standard stars (SPSS), with an internal ~1% precision and tied to Vega within ~3%, for the absolute flux calibration of data gathered by Gaia, the ESA astrometric mission. The criteria for the selection and a list of candidates are presented, together with a description of the survey strategy and the adopted data analysis methods. We also discuss a short list of notable rejected SPSS candidates and difficult cases, based on identification problems, literature discordant data, visual companions, and variability. In fact, all candidates are also monitored for constancy (within  pm5 mmag, approximately). In particular, we report on a CALSPEC standard, 1740346, that we found to be a delta Scuti variable during our short-term monitoring (1-2 h) campaign.

Fueled by both advances in robust optimization theory and applications of reinforcement learning, robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) have gained increasing attention, due to their powerful capability for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. This review provides an in-depth overview of the evolution and advances in RMDPs formulations, particularly in ambiguity modeling, and classifies these methods for representing uncertainty into three principal approaches: parametric, moment-based, and discrepancy-based, elaborating the trade-offs among the alternative representations. Meanwhile, the review delves into the rectangular assumptions, which guarantee the tractability of RMDPs yet are noted for their conservatism. The review summarizes three popular rectangular conditions and develops a new proof to attest to the NP-hardness of non-rectangular RMDPs. Out of the traditional RMDPs scope, recent efforts without conventional rectangular assumptions and new fashions within the RMDPs community are also reviewed. These studies foster the development of more flexible and practical modeling frameworks and enhance the adaptability and performance of RMDPs.

At high-energies the gluon-gluon fusion is the dominant mechanism of $c  bar c$ production. This process was calculated in the NLO collinear as well as in the k$_t$-factorization approaches in the past. We show that the present knowledge of gluon distributions does not allow to make a precise predictions for $c  bar c$ production at LHC, in particular at forward rapidities. In this paper we study production of $c  bar c$ pairs including several subleading mechanisms. This includes: $gg  to Q  bar Q$, $ gamma g  to Q  bar Q$, $g  gamma  to Q  bar Q$, $ gamma  gamma  to Q  bar Q$. In this context we use MRST-QED parton distributions which include photon as a parton in the proton as well as elastic photon distributions calculated in the equivalent photon approximation. We present distributions in the $c$ quark ($ bar c$ antiquark) rapidity and transverse momenta and compare them to the dominant gluon-gluon fusion contribution. We discuss also inclusive single and central diffractive processes using diffractive parton distribution found from the analysis of HERA diffractive data. As in the previous case we present distribution in $c$ ($ bar c$) rapidity and transverse momentum. Finally we present results for exclusive central diffractive mechanism discussed recently in the literature. We show corresponding differential distributions and compare them with corresponding distributions for single and central diffractive components.

Quantum steering, an intermediate quantum correlation lying between entanglement and nonlocality, has emerged as a critical quantum resource for a variety of quantum information processing tasks such as quantum key distribution and true randomness generation. The ability to detect and quantify quantum steering is crucial for these applications. Semi-definite programming (SDP) has proven to be a valuable tool to quantify quantum steering. However, the challenge lies in the fact that the optimal measurement strategy is not priori known, making it time-consuming to compute the steerable measure for any given quantum state. Furthermore, the utilization of SDP requires full information of the quantum state, necessitating quantum state tomography, which can be complex and resource-consuming. In this work, we utilize the semi-supervised self-training model to estimate the steerable weight, a pivotal measure of quantum steering. The model can be trained using a limited amount of labeled data, thus reducing the time for labeling. The features are constructed by the probabilities derived by performing three sets of projective measurements under arbitrary local unitary transformations on the target states, circumventing the need for quantum tomography. The model demonstrates robust generalization capabilities and can achieve high levels of precision with limited resources.

A description is provided of the software algorithms developed for the CMS tracker both for reconstructing charged-particle trajectories in proton-proton interactions and for using the resulting tracks to estimate the positions of the LHC luminous region and individual primary-interaction vertices. Despite the very hostile environment at the LHC, the performance obtained with these algorithms is found to be excellent. For ttbar events under typical 2011 pileup conditions, the average track-reconstruction efficiency for promptly-produced charged particles with transverse momenta of pt > 0.9 GeV is 94% for pseudorapidities of abs(eta) < 0.9 and 85% for 0.9 < abs(eta) < 2.5. The inefficiency is caused mainly by hadrons that undergo nuclear interactions in the tracker material. For isolated muons, the corresponding efficiencies are essentially 100%. For isolated muons of pt = 100 GeV emitted at abs(eta) < 1.4, the resolutions are approximately 2.8% in pt, and respectively, 10 microns and 30 microns in the transverse and longitudinal impact parameters. The position resolution achieved for reconstructed primary vertices that correspond to interesting pp collisions is 10-12 microns in each of the three spatial dimensions. The tracking and vertexing software is fast and flexible, and easily adaptable to other functions, such as fast tracking for the trigger, or dedicated tracking for electrons that takes into account bremsstrahlung.

In smooth and convex multiobjective optimization problems the set of Pareto optima is diffeomorphic to an $m-1$ dimensional simplex, where $m$ is the number of objective functions. The vertices of the simplex are the optima of the individual functions and the $(k-1)$-dimensional facets are the Pareto optimal set of $k$ functions subproblems. Such a hierarchy of submanifolds is a geometrical object called stratification and the union of such manifolds, in this case the set of Pareto optima, is called a stratified set. We discuss how these geometrical structures generalize in the non convex cases, we survey the known results and deduce possible suggestions for the design of dedicated optimization strategies.

In recent years, large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have been pivotal in advancing various artificial intelligence applications, including natural language processing and software engineering. A promising yet underexplored area is utilizing LLMs in software testing, particularly in black-box testing. This paper explores the test cases devised by ChatGPT in comparison to those created by human participants. In this study, ChatGPT (GPT-4) and four participants each created black-box test cases for three applications based on specifications written by the authors. The goal was to evaluate the real-world applicability of the proposed test cases, identify potential shortcomings, and comprehend how ChatGPT could enhance human testing strategies. ChatGPT can generate test cases that generally match or slightly surpass those created by human participants in terms of test viewpoint coverage. Additionally, our experiments demonstrated that when ChatGPT cooperates with humans, it can cover considerably more test viewpoints than each can achieve alone, suggesting that collaboration between humans and ChatGPT may be more effective than human pairs working together. Nevertheless, we noticed that the test cases generated by ChatGPT have certain issues that require addressing before use.

In a previous work of the first authors, a non-holonomic model, generalising the micromorphic models and allowing for curvature (disclinations) to arise from the kinematic values, was presented. In the present paper, a generalisation of the classical models of Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko bending beams based on the mentioned work is proposed. The former is still composed of only one unidimensional scalar field, while the later introduces a third unidimensional scalar field, correcting the second order terms. The generalised Euler-Bernoulli beam is then shown to exhibit curvature (i.e. disclinations) linked to a third order derivative of the displacement, but no torsion (dislocations). Parallelly, the generalised Timoshenko beam is shown to exhibit both curvature and torsion, where the former is linked to the non-holonomy introduced in the generalisation. Lastly, using variational calculus, asymptotic values for the value taken by the curvature in static equilibrium are obtained when the second order contribution becomes negligible; along with an equation for the torsion in the generalised Timoshenko beam.

We consider a Sklyanin algebra S with 3 generators, which is the quadratic algebra over a field k with three generators x,y,z given by three relations pxy+qyx+rzz=0, pyz+qzy+rxx=0 and pzx+qxz+ryy=0, where p,q,r are parameters from the fileld k. This class of algebras enjoyed much of attention, in particular, using tools from algebraic geometry, Feigin & Odesskii, and Artin, Tate & Van den Berg, showed that if at least two of the parameters p, q and r are non-zero and at least two of three numbers p^3,q^3 and r^3 are distinct, then S is Koszul and has the same Hilbert series as the algebra of commutative polynomials in three variables. It became commonly accepted, that it is impossible to achieve the same objective by purely algebraic and combinatorial means, like the Groebner basis technique. The main purpose of this paper is to trace combinatorial meaning of the properties of Sklyanin algebras, such as Koszulity, PBW, PHS, Calabi-Yau, and to give a new constructive proof of the above facts due to Artin, Tate and Van den Bergh.   Further, we study a wider class of Sklyanin algebras, namely the situation when all parameters of relations could be different. This class called generalized Sklyanin algebras. We classify up to isomorphism genralized Sklyanin algebras with polynomial Hilbert series. We show that generalized Slyanin algebras in general position have the Golod-Shafarevich Hilbert series (with exception of the case of the field with two elements).

In this paper, we review observational aspects of three common small-scale energetic events in the solar transition region (TR), namely: TR explosive events, ultraviolet bursts and jets. These events are defined in either (both) spectral or (and) imaging data. The development of multiple instruments capable of observing the TR has allowed researchers to gain numerous insights into these phenomena in recent years. These events have provided a proxy to study how mass and energy are transported between the solar chromosphere and the corona. As the physical mechanisms responsible for these small-scale events might be similar to the mechanisms responsible for large-scale phenomena, such as flares and coronal mass ejections, analysis of these events could also help our understanding of the solar atmosphere from small to large scales. The observations of these small-scale energetic events demonstrate that the TR is extremely dynamic and is a crucial layer in the solar atmosphere between the chromosphere and the corona.

Wearable egocentric cameras and machine learning have the potential to provide clinicians with a more nuanced understanding of patient hand use at home after stroke and spinal cord injury (SCI). However, they require detailed contextual information (i.e., activities and object interactions) to effectively interpret metrics and meaningfully guide therapy planning. We demonstrate that an object-centric approach, focusing on what objects patients interact with rather than how they move, can effectively recognize Activities of Daily Living (ADL) in real-world rehabilitation settings. We evaluated our models on a complex dataset collected in the wild comprising 2261 minutes of egocentric video from 16 participants with impaired hand function. By leveraging pre-trained object detection and hand-object interaction models, our system achieves robust performance across different impairment levels and environments, with our best model achieving a mean weighted F1-score of 0.78 +/- 0.12 and maintaining an F1-score > 0.5 for all participants using leave-one-subject-out cross validation. Through qualitative analysis, we observe that this approach generates clinically interpretable information about functional object use while being robust to patient-specific movement variations, making it particularly suitable for rehabilitation contexts with prevalent upper limb impairment.

We analytically prove that the existence of the delta-function singularity in the chirally-odd twist-3 distribution $e(x)$ of the nucleon is inseparably connected with the nonvanishing quark condensate as a signal of the spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking of the QCD vacuum. This singularity in $e(x)$, which would be observed as a sizable violation of the 1st moment sum rule, is then interpreted as giving a very rare case that the nontrivial vacuum structure of QCD manifests in an observable of a localized QCD excitation, i.e. the nucleon.

Functional data analysis has been extensively conducted. In this study, we consider a partially functional model, under which some covariates are scalars and have linear effects, while some other variables are functional and have unspecified nonlinear effects. Significantly advancing from the existing literature, we consider a model with interactions between the functional and scalar covariates. To accommodate long-tailed error distributions which are not uncommon in data analysis, we adopt the quantile technique for estimation. To achieve more interpretable estimation, and to accommodate many practical settings, we assume that the functional covariate effects are locally sparse (that is, there exist subregions on which the effects are exactly zero), which naturally leads to a variable/model selection problem. We propose respecting the  main effect, interaction  hierarchy, which postulates that if a subregion has a nonzero effect in an interaction term, then its effect has to be nonzero in the corresponding main functional effect. For estimation, identification of local sparsity, and respect of the hierarchy, we propose a penalization approach. An effective computational algorithm is developed, and the consistency properties are rigorously established under mild regularity conditions. Simulation shows the practical effectiveness of the proposed approach. The analysis of the Tecator data further demonstrates its practical applicability. Overall, this study can deliver a novel and practically useful model and a statistically and numerically satisfactory estimation approach.

A commonly used technique for managing AI complexity in real-time strategy (RTS) games is to use action and/or state abstractions. High-level abstractions can often lead to good strategic decision making, but tactical decision quality may suffer due to lost details. A competing method is to sample the search space which often leads to good tactical performance in simple scenarios, but poor high-level planning.   We propose to use a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to select among a limited set of abstract action choices, and to utilize the remaining computation time for game tree search to improve low level tactics. The CNN is trained by supervised learning on game states labelled by Puppet Search, a strategic search algorithm that uses action abstractions. The network is then used to select a script --- an abstract action --- to produce low level actions for all units. Subsequently, the game tree search algorithm improves the tactical actions of a subset of units using a limited view of the game state only considering units close to opponent units.   Experiments in the microRTS game show that the combined algorithm results in higher win-rates than either of its two independent components and other state-of-the-art microRTS agents.   To the best of our knowledge, this is the first successful application of a convolutional network to play a full RTS game on standard game maps, as previous work has focused on sub-problems, such as combat, or on very small maps.

Tool learning has emerged as a promising direction by extending Large Language Models' (LLMs) capabilities with external tools. Existing tool learning studies primarily focus on the general-purpose tool-use capability, which addresses explicit user requirements in instructions. However, they overlook the importance of personalized tool-use capability, leading to an inability to handle implicit user preferences. To address the limitation, we first formulate the task of personalized tool learning, which integrates user's interaction history towards personalized tool usage. To fill the gap of missing benchmarks, we construct PEToolBench, featuring diverse user preferences reflected in interaction history under three distinct personalized settings, and encompassing a wide range of tool-use scenarios. Moreover, we propose a framework PEToolLLaMA to adapt LLMs to the personalized tool learning task, which is trained through supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. Extensive experiments on PEToolBench demonstrate the superiority of PEToolLLaMA over existing LLMs.

Renewable energy sources and further electrificationof energy consumption are key enablers for decreasing green-house gas emissions, but also introduce increased complexitywithin the electric power system. The increased availability ofautomation, information and communication technology, andintelligent solutions for system operation have transformed thepower system into a smart grid. In order to support thedevelopment process of smart grid solutions on the system level,testing has to be done in a holistic manner, covering the multi-domain aspect of such complex systems. This paper introducesthe concept of holistic power system testing and discuss first stepstowards a corresponding methodology that is being developed inthe European ERIGrid research infrastructure project.

We propose a new procedure for parton-to-hadron fragmentation in proton-proton collisions. The hadronization is considered in the parton-parton center-of-mass system and hadrons are assumed to be emitted in the direction of outgoing partons in that frame and then their four-momenta are transformed to the overall center-of-mass system using relevant Lorentz transformations and appropriate distributions are constructed. For heavy hadron production the energy-momentum condition is imposed. In many cases our procedure disagrees with the commonly used rule that rapidity of produced hadron is the same as rapidity of the parent parton. We illustrate the newly proposed scheme for production of $D$ mesons, $ Lambda_c$ baryon and $ eta_c$ quarkonium in leading-order approach to parton production. The transverse momentum, rapidity and Feynman-$x_F$ distributions are shown. We consider $c  to D$ and $g  to D$ as well as $c  to  eta_c$ and $g  to  eta_c$ hadronization processes. The resulting rapidity distributions are much narrower than those obtained in the traditional approach with parton-hadron rapidity equivalence. This has consequences both for mid- and forward rapidities and could have consequences for high-energy neutrino production in the Earth's atmosphere. We discuss also $c  to  Lambda_c^+$ and $b  to  Lambda_c^+$ fragmentation and find that the second mechanism could be partly responsible for the enhanced production of $ Lambda_c^{ pm}$ observed recently by the ALICE collaboration.

Robust and generalized tool manipulation requires an understanding of the properties and affordances of different tools. We investigate whether linguistic information about a tool (e.g., its geometry, common uses) can help control policies adapt faster to new tools for a given task. We obtain diverse descriptions of various tools in natural language and use pre-trained language models to generate their feature representations. We then perform language-conditioned meta-learning to learn policies that can efficiently adapt to new tools given their corresponding text descriptions. Our results demonstrate that combining linguistic information and meta-learning significantly accelerates tool learning in several manipulation tasks including pushing, lifting, sweeping, and hammering.

The dynamics of two-level systems in time-dependent backgrounds is under consideration. We present some new exact solutions in special backgrounds decaying in time. On the other hand, following ideas of Feynman, Vernon and Hellwarth, we discuss in detail the possibility to reduce the quantum dynamics to a classical Hamiltonian system. This, in particular, opens the possibility to directly apply powerful methods of classical mechanics (e.g. KAM methods) to study the quantum system. Following such an approach, we draw conclusions of relevance for ``quantum chaos'' when the external background is periodic or quasi-periodic in time.

We find an exact solution of the equations of motion of a two-field cosmological model, which realizes multi-field dark energy. The latter is characterized by field-space trajectories with turning rates that are always large. We study a class of two-field models and show that it is possible to have such trajectories, giving accelerated space-time expansion, even when the scalar potential preserves the rotational invariance of the field-space metric. For the case of Poincar 'e-disk field space, we derive the form of the scalar potential compatible with such background solutions and, furthermore, we find the exact solutions analytically. Their field-space trajectories are spirals inward, toward the center of the Poincar 'e disk. Interestingly, the functional form of the relevant scalar potential is compatible with a certain hidden symmetry, although the latter is broken by the presence of a constant term.

Mechanical defects in real situations affect observation values and cause abnormalities in multivariate time series, such as sensor values or network data. To perceive abnormalities in such data, it is crucial to understand the temporal context and interrelation between variables simultaneously. The anomaly detection task for time series, especially for unlabeled data, has been a challenging problem, and we address it by applying a suitable data degradation scheme to self-supervised model training. We define four types of synthetic outliers and propose the degradation scheme in which a portion of input data is replaced with one of the synthetic outliers. Inspired by the self-attention mechanism, we design a Transformer-based architecture to recognize the temporal context and detect unnatural sequences with high efficiency. Our model converts multivariate data points into temporal representations with relative position bias and yields anomaly scores from these representations. Our method, AnomalyBERT, shows a great capability of detecting anomalies contained in complex time series and surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods on five real-world benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jhryu30/AnomalyBERT.

The increasing demand for controllable outputs in text-to-image generation has spurred advancements in multi-instance generation (MIG), allowing users to define both instance layouts and attributes. However, unlike image-conditional generation methods such as ControlNet, MIG techniques have not been widely adopted in state-of-the-art models like SD2 and SDXL, primarily due to the challenge of building robust renderers that simultaneously handle instance positioning and attribute rendering. In this paper, we introduce Depth-Driven Decoupled Instance Synthesis (3DIS), a novel framework that decouples the MIG process into two stages: (i) generating a coarse scene depth map for accurate instance positioning and scene composition, and (ii) rendering fine-grained attributes using pre-trained ControlNet on any foundational model, without additional training. Our 3DIS framework integrates a custom adapter into LDM3D for precise depth-based layouts and employs a finetuning-free method for enhanced instance-level attribute rendering. Extensive experiments on COCO-Position and COCO-MIG benchmarks demonstrate that 3DIS significantly outperforms existing methods in both layout precision and attribute rendering. Notably, 3DIS offers seamless compatibility with diverse foundational models, providing a robust, adaptable solution for advanced multi-instance generation. The code is available at: https://github.com/limuloo/3DIS.
rewritten: Let C represent a coalgebra defined over a field k, with A denoting its corresponding dual algebra. The category of C-comodules can be equated to a category of A-modules. This equivalence allows us to understand the cotensor product M square N of two comodules in relation to the relevant Hochschild cohomology of the A-bimodule M tensor N. This interpretation holds true when A possesses characteristics such as being finite-dimensional, profinite, graded, or differential-graded. The primary areas where these concepts find application are in Galois cohomology, comodules associated with the Steenrod algebra, and the homology analysis of induced fibrations.

It is a common occurrence that the introduction of a new concept or idea often triggers the emergence of subsequent related innovations, which is a well-recognized aspect of daily life. This phenomenon is believed to play a crucial role in the development of biological systems, human society, and technology. Termed as "expanding the adjacent possible" by Kauffman, this process involves one novelty creating opportunities for the emergence of others. Despite the significance of correlated novelties, there is a lack of empirical quantification and mathematical modeling to understand its dynamics.

In this study, we present a straightforward mathematical model that simulates the exploration of physical, biological, or conceptual spaces that expand with each novelty. Drawing inspiration from Polya's urn model, our generalized approach predicts statistical patterns regarding the frequency of novelty occurrences (similar to Heaps' law) and the distribution of novelties within the explored space (analogous to Zipf's law). Additionally, our model offers insights into how one novelty can pave the way for subsequent innovations. To validate our model, we analyze four datasets related to human activities: Wikipedia page edits, tag emergence in annotation systems, word sequences in texts, and new song listening habits on online music platforms.

By quantitatively assessing the dynamics of correlated novelties, our findings serve as a foundational framework for gaining a deeper comprehension of the continuous expansion of the adjacent possible and its influence on biological, linguistic, cultural, and technological advancements.

The primary pomeron loop at the lowest order has been computed for the principal conformal weight, incorporating the complete influence of the triple pomeron vertex on intermediary conformal weights. It has been determined that the loop converges. Its impact on the pomeron Green function becomes significant at rapidities between 10 and 15. The pomeron pole renormalization is observed to be minimal, attributed to the swift decrease in the triple pomeron vertex as the conformal weights increase.

We demonstrate that $ \mu(\mathcal{L}) \lambda_1(\mathcal{L}^*) < (0.1275 + o(1)) \cdot n$, where $ \mu(\mathcal{L})$ represents the covering radius of an $n$-dimensional lattice $ \mathcal{L} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and $ \lambda_1(\mathcal{L}^*)$ denotes the length of the shortest non-zero vector in the dual lattice $ \mathcal{L}^*$. This enhancement surpasses Banaszczyk's well-known transference theorem (Math. Annal., 1993) by roughly 20%. Our proof closely aligns with Banaszczyk's argument, with the exception of a specific step where we substitute a Fourier-analytic estimate on discrete Gaussian mass with a marginally stronger estimate grounded on packing. The packing-based estimate we apply has previously been established by Aggarwal, Dadush, Regev, and Stephens-Davidowitz (STOC, 2015) in a distinct context. Consequently, our contribution lies in recognizing that this leads to an improved transference theorem.

This study examines the impact of orienting external fields on pattern formation, specifically mesoscale turbulence, in suspensions of microswimmers. To achieve this, we utilize a hydrodynamic theory derived from a microscopic model of microswimmers [Phys. Rev. E 97, 022613 (2018)]. The theory integrates a dynamic equation for the polar order parameter with a modified Stokes equation for the flow of the solvent. In this study, we enhance the model by introducing an external field that applies an aligning torque to the swimmers, simulating scenarios such as chemo-, photo-, magneto-, or gravitaxis. 

In contrast to the absence of an external field, the introduction of an external field disrupts the rotational symmetry of vortex dynamics and results in distinctly asymmetric, traveling stripe patterns. This phenomenon is illustrated through numerical solutions and linear stability analysis. Additionally, we analyze these emerging structures using a simplified model that focuses solely on an (effective) velocity field of microswimmers. While this model is more manageable for analytical purposes, it still captures the essential characteristics of asymmetric pattern formation. We observe a transition from a square vortex lattice to a traveling stripe pattern underlying these structures. These patterns can be effectively explained within the framework of weakly nonlinear analysis, assuming that the influence of nonlinear advection remains sufficiently weak.

The emergence of wide-area submillimeter surveys has unveiled a significant number of high-redshift gravitationally lensed dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs). The straightforward selection criteria for potential lensed sources in these surveys, identified as those with $S_{500 mu m} > 100$ mJy, eliminate uncertainties related to the selection function modeling. This unique combination makes submillimeter surveys perfect for investigating strong lens statistics. To explore the lensing statistics of submillimeter-selected sources, we conducted a preliminary study by observing a sample of strongly-lensed sources with the Atacama Large Millimetre Array (ALMA), chosen from surveys conducted with the Herschel Space Observatory. We attempted to replicate the distribution of image separations for the lensed sources using a halo mass function from a numerical simulation that includes both dark matter and baryons. Three different density distributions were utilized, including one based on analytical fits to the halos formed in the EAGLE simulation, and two density distributions (Singular Isothermal Sphere (SIS) and SISSA) previously used in lensing studies. Our findings indicate that all three density distributions could replicate the observed distribution by implementing an upper mass transition of $ sim$$10^{13} M_{odot}$ for the SIS and SISSA models, beyond which an NFW profile could represent the density distribution. We demonstrated that a sample size of approximately 500 lensed sources would be necessary to differentiate between the density distributions, a feasible task considering the expected number of lensed sources in Herschel surveys.

We establish the supersymmetric extension of E$_{6(6)}$-covariant extraordinary field theory. This theory is founded on a generalized space-time of dimensions $(5+27)$, which is governed by a covariant section restriction. The fermions within this framework are characterized as tensors within the local Lorentz group ${\rm SO}(1,4) \times {\rm USp}(8)$ and undergo transformations as weighted scalars within the E$_{6(6)}$ (internal) generalized diffeomorphisms. A comprehensive Lagrangian is presented, demonstrating its consistency with supersymmetry. By resolving the section constraint explicitly, the theory encompasses complete $D=11$ supergravity and IIB supergravity, respectively.

Recent studies have shown that the phenomenological Tsallis fits to the transverse momentum spectra of hadrons in pp collisions at the LHC, as measured by CMS, ATLAS, and ALICE, cover a wide range of transverse momentum values. We aim to understand if the simplicity of the Tsallis parametrization can be linked to relativistic parton-parton hard-scattering and related phenomena. Our analysis focuses on the impact of multiple hard-scattering and parton showering processes on the power law behavior. Our empirical findings reveal that while both hadrons and jets exhibit power-law behavior at high transverse momenta (pT), the power indices for hadrons are consistently higher than those for jets, with values around n~4-5.

We present a new method for generating human-object interactions (HOIs) guided by text, which effectively models interactions at the joint level in a computationally efficient manner. Previous approaches represented the entire human body as a single entity, limiting the ability to capture detailed joint-level interactions and resulting in unrealistic HOIs. Conversely, representing each joint as an individual entity would significantly increase the number of tokens, leading to higher computational costs. To tackle these challenges, we introduce the Efficient Explicit Joint-level Interaction Model (EJIM). EJIM includes a Dual-branch HOI Mamba that efficiently models spatiotemporal HOI information separately, along with a Dual-branch Condition Injector that incorporates text semantics and object geometry into human and object movements. Additionally, we introduce a Dynamic Interaction Block and a progressive masking mechanism to filter out irrelevant joints iteratively, ensuring precise and nuanced interaction modeling. Through thorough quantitative and qualitative evaluations on public datasets, we demonstrate that EJIM outperforms previous methods by a substantial margin while maintaining only 5% of the inference time. The code can be accessed at this  href{https://github.com/Huanggh531/EJIM}{link}.

After analyzing dilepton rates and electrical conductivity from continuum extrapolated results of light quark correlation functions in quenched QCD, I will provide an overview of recent advancements in lattice QCD research on quarkonia in the quark gluon plasma. The discussion will include recent improvements in determining spectral properties from lattice QCD calculations of hadronic correlation functions. In addition to examining medium-induced changes in bound states and their dissolution in the plasma, I will explore transport coefficients such as heavy quark diffusion constants derived from various correlation functions on the lattice. The presentation will also touch upon current limitations and future prospects for investigating quarkonia and related transport coefficients using lattice techniques.

We analyze the dynamics of a directed manifold in a random force field with internal dimension D and d dimensions. An exact solution is derived for $d  to  infty$, while a Hartree approximation is used for finite d. These solutions reveal a Flory-like roughness exponent $ zeta$ and a non-trivial anomalous diffusion exponent $ nu$ that vary continuously based on the ratio $g_{T}/g_{L}$ of divergence-free ($g_{T}$) to potential ($g_{L}$) disorder strength. When D=0, our findings align with previous order $ epsilon^2$ RG calculations. The time-translational invariant dynamics transition smoothly from $g_{T} >0$ to the ultrametric aging solution in the potential case.

This report outlines the final project completed to meet the requirements for the M.Sc. degree in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Ben-Gurion University (BGU) of the Negev. The project focuses on theoretical research into natural convection compressible flow with high temperature differences and complex geometries. The research is motivated by ongoing investigations into steady state and transient multiphase flow regimes within the reactor core at the Soreq Nuclear Center. The primary aim is to develop a numerical methodology for modeling natural convection compressible flow using standard computational fluid dynamics (CFD) techniques such as pressure-based solution algorithms and immersed boundary methods. The report includes a thorough literature review of simulation methods for natural convection flow and immersed boundary methods, an outline of research objectives, a detailed physical model with governing equations, constitutive laws, and dimensional analysis. It also features a verification study comparing results with existing numerical data for incompressible and non-Boussinesq compressible flows without complex geometry, a comparison of results with previous studies for configurations with low temperature differences and complex geometry, a solution and analysis of configurations with high temperature differences and complex geometry, and concludes with a summary, conclusions, and recommendations for future work.

In the context of a ring $R$, our focus is on examining bimodules $M$ that result in a morphic trivial extension $R \boxtimes M$. A comprehensive characterization is achieved specifically when $R$ is deemed left perfect. Furthermore, we demonstrate the morphic nature of $R \boxtimes Q/R$ in scenarios where $R$ is a commutative reduced ring with a classical ring of quotients denoted as $Q". Additionally, we expand upon existing findings related to the correlation between morphic rings and unit regular rings.

Various findings regarding the cascade power in robust, incompressible MHD turbulence with non-zero cross helicity have been documented in scholarly works. This study aims to elucidate the conditions under which these diverse outcomes hold true. We introduce z+ as the root mean square (rms) amplitude of Alfven waves traveling parallel to the background magnetic field, and z- as the rms amplitude of Alfven waves traveling in the opposite direction. Non-zero cross helicity signifies a disparity between z+ and z-, with z- being smaller than z+. Our analysis reveals that the generation process of z- fluctuations significantly impacts the cascade power by influencing the coherence time for interactions between wave packets with opposite directions at the largest scale. Specifically, when maintaining constant values for z+ and z-, the cascade power tends to be higher in scenarios where z- fluctuations arise from reflecting z+ fluctuations compared to cases where forcing weakly correlates with z+ fluctuations.

The paper introduces a novel technique for transmitting secret messages or images using (2, 2) visual cryptographic shares that are generally non-interpretable. Initially, a binary image serves as the cover image, with an authenticating message or image embedded into it using a hash function. This process involves embedding two bits in each pixel within four bits from the least significant bit (LSB), resulting in the conversion of the binary image to a grayscale version. Subsequently, (2,2) visual cryptographic shares are derived from this grayscale image. Upon decoding, these shares are combined to reconstruct the authenticated image, enabling retrieval of the secret message or image through the same hash function while minimizing noise. Additionally, noise reduction techniques are applied to the reconstructed authenticated image to restore the original cover image at the intended destination.

By utilizing fluorescence microscopy, we investigate the adsorption behavior of individual latex microparticles at a water/water interface within demixing aqueous polymer solutions, commonly referred to as a water-in-water emulsion. In contrast to similar microparticles at interfaces between molecular liquids which demonstrate a notably sluggish relaxation process, hindering the observation of anticipated equilibrium states, this sluggishness has been linked to persistent metastable states due to substantial energy barriers ($ Delta{ cal F} sim  gamma A_d gg k_B T$). These barriers are induced by high interfacial tension ($ gamma  sim 10^{-2}$ N/m) and nanoscale surface defects with characteristic areas of $A_d  simeq$ 10--30 nm$^2$. 

In our examination of the water/water interface with an exceptionally low surface tension ($ gamma  sim 10^{-4}$ N/m), we can thoroughly analyze the entire adsorption process and witness equilibrium states defined by a single equilibrium contact angle that remains constant regardless of particle size. Interestingly, transitions from rapid initial dynamics to slower kinetic phases, as predicted analytically for substantial surface defects ($A_d  simeq$ 500 nm$^2$), are observed. Additionally, the trajectories of the particles reveal a damping coefficient independent of position, contrary to expectations considering the substantial viscosity contrast between the phases. These findings are attributed to the diffuse nature of the water/water interface and the adsorption and entanglement of polymer chains within semidilute solutions. This research provides initial insights into the dynamics and kinetics of microparticle adsorption at water/water interfaces in bio-colloidal systems.

Our research focused on examining the stability and superconductivity of FeSe nanosheets throughout the process of device fabrication in air. We devised techniques to enhance the exfoliation efficiency and preserve the superconducting properties of FeSe. Analysis through Raman spectroscopy, atomic force microscopy, optical microscopy, and time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry indicated that FeSe nanosheets deteriorated when exposed to air, potentially due to Se particle precipitation and iron oxidation. Furthermore, conventional electron beam lithography was found to diminish the superconducting behavior of FeSe. However, our study demonstrated that utilizing shadow mask evaporation and transferring onto predetermined electrodes were effective strategies in maintaining the superconductivity post-fabrication. These innovative methods offer a pathway for producing high-quality FeSe nano-devices.

We investigate an enhancement of the $q,t$-Catalan numbers as introduced by Xin and Zhang (2022, 2023) through the utilization of polyhedral geometry tools. These refined $q,t$-Catalan numbers are contingent upon a parameter vector $ \mathbf{k}$, with the conventional $q,t$-Catalan numbers emerging when $ \mathbf{k} = (1, \ldots, 1)$. The interpretation of Xin and Zhang's generating functions is facilitated by the development of polyhedral cones that stem from constraints imposed on $ \mathbf{k}$-Dyck paths, along with their associated area and bounce statistics. By employing this polyhedral methodology, we are able to establish Xin and Zhang's theorem regarding the $q,t$-symmetry of the refined $q,t$-Catalan numbers in instances where $ \mathbf{k} = (k_1, k_2, k_3)$ and $(k, k, k, k)$, provide extensions such as when $ \mathbf{k} = (k, k+m, k+m, k+m)$, and explore connections with other variations of the $q,t$-Catalan numbers.

In the confinement phase of SU(2) lattice gauge theory, it is observed that P-Vortices tend to aggregate into a single extensive percolating cluster in the infrared range, alongside several smaller clusters in the ultraviolet range. The correlation between monopole clusters in the maximal Abelian projection and P-vortex clusters is examined. Extraction of P-vortices is conducted through direct and indirect central projections, yielding comparable outcomes.

Let G be a closed and transitive subgroup of the group of homeomorphisms on the circle, denoted as Homeo(S^1), that includes a non-constant continuous mapping f: [0,1] --> G. It can be demonstrated that, in terms of conjugation, G falls into one of the following categories: SO(2,R), PSL(2,R), PSL_k(2,R), Homeo_k(S^1), or Homeo(S^1). This result confirms the classification proposed by Ghys in the publication "Enseign. Math. 47 (2001) 329-407".

As a consequence of this analysis, it can be concluded that the group PSL(2,R) represents a maximal closed subgroup within Homeo(S^1) (a conjecture attributed to de la Harpe). Furthermore, it is revealed that if a subgroup G < Homeo(S^1) exhibits continuous transitive action on k-tuples of points, where k>3, then the closure of G corresponds to Homeo(S^1) (referencing Bestvina's compilation of 'Questions in geometric group theory').

The EPIC CCD cameras aboard XMM-Newton discovered a 54 mHz quasiperiodic oscillation (QPO) in the X-ray flux above 2 keV from an ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX) in the starburst galaxy M82. This finding marks the first identification of a QPO in the X-ray flux from an extragalactic ULX, confirming its compact nature. While it is likely associated with the most luminous object in the central region of M82, CXOM82 J095550.2+694047, XMM imaging alone cannot definitively confirm this. The alternative candidate, CXOM82 J095551.1+694045, seems less probable due to the comparison of QPO luminosity with peak luminosity in Chandra observations.

The QPO had a centroid frequency of 54.3 +- 0.9 mHz, a coherence of 5, and an amplitude (rms) of 8.5% in the 2 - 10 keV band. Below 0.2 Hz, the power spectrum follows a power-law with an index ~1 and an amplitude (rms) of 13.5%. The X-ray spectrum is best described by a curving continuum, with a disk-blackbody (diskbb) at T = 3.1 keV providing a satisfactory fit. A broad Fe line at 6.55 keV is consistently needed in all fits, but the equivalent width (EW) depends on the continuum model used, with no indication of a reflection component. The estimated bolometric luminosity is around 4 - 5 x 10^{40} ergs/sec.

Additionally, archival Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) observations at M82 also suggest QPOs in the frequency range of 50 - 100 mHz. Our findings have significant implications for ULX models.

Due to the constraints of traditional silicon-based computing technology, various unconventional computing methods have been suggested as alternatives. Among these, DNA computing has emerged as a promising option due to its significant advantages in terms of parallel processing, information storage capacity, speed, and energy efficiency. This study will specifically delve into the application of DNA computing for syllogistic reasoning, illustrating how the use of DNA tweezers can be interpreted through the semantics of process calculus and DNA strand graphs. Syllogistic reasoning plays a crucial role in the common sense logic of individuals, and this research elucidates the systematic approach to deriving precise conclusions from a set of propositions by leveraging the formal language theory inherent in process calculus and the expressive capabilities of DNA strand graphs.

We demonstrate how an ion trap, designed for coherent manipulation of external and internal quantum states, can simulate the irreversible dynamics of the Dicke model, a collective angular momentum model. Specifically, in the scenario involving two ions, entanglement is generated in the coherently driven steady state with linear driving. For cases with more than two ions, we compute the entanglement between two ions in the Dicke model's steady state by averaging over all other ions. The maximum entanglement in the steady state occurs at parameter values approximately corresponding to a bifurcation of a fixed point in the semiclassical dynamics. We propose that this mechanism is a general method for creating entanglement in driven dissipative quantum systems.

Visual place recognition (VPR) is essential for robots to recognize familiar locations, a critical component for independent navigation indoors and outdoors. However, current VPR datasets mostly focus on single viewpoints, resulting in lower accuracy in scenarios with multiple directions or few distinguishing features. Acquiring additional data to address these limitations can be costly. This study presents a new training method to enhance existing VPR networks by increasing multi-view diversity within current datasets through uncertainty estimation and NeRF-based data augmentation. Initially, we train NeRF using the existing VPR dataset. A self-supervised uncertainty estimation network then identifies places with high uncertainty, utilizing their poses to generate new synthetic observations through NeRF for further VPR network training. Moreover, we propose an improved storage system for efficient management of augmented and original training data. Extensive experiments were conducted on three datasets using three distinct VPR backbone networks. The results illustrate the significant enhancement in VPR performance achieved by our training method, surpassing other approaches. Validation on self-recorded indoor and outdoor datasets consistently demonstrated superior outcomes. Our dataset and code are available at  href{https://github.com/nubot-nudt/UGNA-VPR}{https://github.com/nubot-nudt/UGNA-VPR}.

This paper presents diffusion equation models in the spectral domain for analyzing the training error evolution of two-layer multi-scale deep neural networks (MscaleDNN). The aim is to address the spectral bias issue in fully connected deep neural networks when approximating oscillatory functions. The diffusion models are derived from the spectral form of the error equation of MscaleDNN using a neural tangent kernel approach, gradient descent training, and a sine activation function. This derivation assumes a vanishing learning rate, infinite network width, and domain size. The diffusion coefficients involved exhibit larger supports with an increase in the number of scales used in MscaleDNN. Consequently, the proposed diffusion equation models in the frequency domain elucidate the spectral bias reduction capability of MscaleDNN. Numerical results of the diffusion models for training a two-layer MscaleDNN align with the error evolution observed in actual gradient descent training with a sufficiently large network width, validating the efficacy of the diffusion models. Furthermore, the numerical findings for MscaleDNN demonstrate error reduction across a broad frequency spectrum, underscoring the advantage of utilizing MscaleDNN for approximating functions with diverse frequency ranges.

This paper focuses on compactifications of manifolds. Siebenmann's seminal dissertation defined open manifolds M^m (m>5) that can be compactified by introducing a manifold boundary. This theorem easily applies to cases where M^m is noncompact with a compact boundary; however, it becomes more complex when Bd(M^m) is noncompact. The objective shifts to completing M^m, creating a compact manifold C^m and a compact subset A such that C^m A = M^m. While Siebenmann and O'Brien made initial contributions to this topic, a comprehensive characterization was lacking until now, which we provide. Our second main theorem deals with Z-compactifications. A pending question is whether the conditions set forth by Chapman and Siebenmann ensure Z-compactifiability for a manifold M^m. Although we cannot definitively answer this question, we demonstrate that these conditions are met if and only if M x [0,1] is Z-compactifiable. An essential component is the Manifold Completion Theorem mentioned above, which in part explains our current focus on this topic and showcases the practicality of the conditions outlined in that theorem.

We introduce a model-agnostic framework for generating prediction intervals for insurance claims, offering finite sample statistical assurances. This framework extends the split conformal prediction method to two-stage frequency-severity modeling. The efficacy of the framework is demonstrated through experiments with both simulated and actual datasets, employing traditional parametric models and modern machine learning techniques. In cases where a random forest serves as the underlying severity model, we enhance the two-stage split conformal prediction algorithm. This enhancement showcases how the out-of-bag mechanism can eliminate the necessity for a calibration set in the conformal procedure.

We have computed the high-temperature series for the specific heat and structure factor of the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the Kagome lattice. Comparing the series with exact diagonalization studies reveals that, in addition to a prominent peak around $T \approx \frac{2}{3}$, the specific heat exhibits additional structure at lower temperatures. The structure factor at $T=0.25$ closely aligns with findings for the ground state of a finite cluster comprising 36 sites. Notably, at this temperature, the structure factor is less than twice its value at $T=\infty$ and demonstrates weak dependence on the wavevector $\mathbf{q}$, suggesting the absence of magnetic order and a correlation length shorter than one lattice spacing. The uniform susceptibility peaks around $T \approx \frac{1}{6}$ before exponentially diminishing at lower temperatures.

Forced convection cooling plays a crucial role in various technologies, such as microprocessors in data centers and turbines or engines, where active cooling is necessary. However, the active transfer of heat or thermal energy under a significant temperature difference results in the rapid destruction of exergy, the free-energy component of thermal energy. This issue has yet to be addressed. 

In this study, we propose a thermoelectrochemical conversion method to partially recover the lost exergy in forced convection cooling processes. A test cell is designed, wherein an electrolyte liquid is pushed through a channel formed between two parallel electrodes, with the hot-side electrode mimicking the object to be cooled. Our findings indicate that narrower interelectrode channels lead to improved cooling and power generation performance.

Across all tested conditions, mass transfer resistance emerges as the most dominant resistance type, with charge transfer kinetics likely being influenced by viscosity. The variation in the generated power with flow rate is attributed to changes in the diffusion coefficient of redox species with temperature. To evaluate these forced-flow thermocells, we introduce a metric called gain (Lambda), representing the ratio of generated power to the hydrodynamic pumping work needed to propel the liquid through the cell. In a specific flow rate range, Lambda exceeds unity, indicating that the system can produce more electric power than the pump work required, thereby hinting at its potential to partially recover lost exergy from thermal energy in the form of electricity.

We conducted shell model calculations on the beta-decay of the 14C ground state to the 14N ground state, considering the states of the A=14 multiplet as two 0p holes within a 16O core. Utilizing low-momentum nucleon-nucleon (NN) interactions based on the Bonn-B potential, we observed that the Gamow-Teller matrix element was too large to accurately represent the known lifetime. However, upon utilizing a modified version of this potential that includes Brown-Rho scaling medium modifications, we discovered that the GT matrix element becomes negligible at a nuclear density approximately 85% of nuclear matter. Furthermore, we found that the medium-modified Bonn-B potential enhances the splitting between the (J,T)=(1+,0) and (J,T)=(0+,1) states in 14N, while also showing that the transition strengths from excited states of 14C to the 14N ground state align well with recent experimental findings.

In the past decade, there has been a significant focus on the critical dynamics of cortical neurons. Neuronal avalanches have emerged as key tools, both experimentally and theoretically, for studying criticality in such systems. Experimental findings indicate that critical neuronal avalanches exhibit mean-field characteristics. Various structural and recently proposed dynamical mechanisms, as referenced in Phys. Rev. E 89, 052139 (2014), have been identified as potential contributors to this mean-field behavior. This study explores a straightforward model of neuronal dynamics rooted in threshold self-organized critical models with synaptic noise. The investigation delves into the impact of high average connectivity, random long-range connections, and synaptic noise on achieving mean-field behavior. Finite-size scaling is utilized to accurately determine critical exponents. The study concludes that while structural mechanisms relevant to mean-field behavior may not align with realistic cortical models, significant dynamical noise – with plausible justifications – consistently results in mean-field behavior regardless of the underlying structure. This research offers a distinct (dynamical) perspective on the origin of mean-field behavior in neuronal avalanches, challenging the traditionally accepted (structural) mechanisms.

In spin-density-functional theory (SDFT) for noncollinear magnetic materials, the Kohn-Sham system involves exchange-correlation (xc) scalar potentials and magnetic fields. The xc magnetic fields, which can induce local torques on magnetization, are not thoroughly explored. Exact benchmark solutions for a five-site extended Hubbard lattice at half filling with spin-orbit coupling are compared with SDFT results using orbital-dependent exchange-only approximations. The exchange-only approximation adequately describes magnetization dynamics after short-pulse excitations for weak to moderate interactions. However, for stronger interactions near transitions between magnetically ordered and frustrated phases, both exchange and correlation torques need to be considered as they tend to offset each other.

A recent experimental report indicated that monolayer graphene can be doped beyond the Van Hove singularity. Our theoretical study focuses on exploring potential superconductivity and associated spin excitations in this doping range of monolayer graphene. A static spin-density-wave state is deemed favorable, attributed to the nested Fermi surface resulting from doping the Fermi level to the Van Hove singularity point. Further doping could potentially lead to the realization of superconductivity. Theoretical examination of spin excitations in the superconducting state is conducted using the random phase approximation method. Notably, the general characteristics are found to be qualitatively similar to those observed in cuprate superconductors. As a result, we propose an intriguing possibility that heavily overdoped monolayer graphene could serve as a unique platform for investigating unconventional superconductivity.

We present a straightforward model elucidating the phenomenon of time-reversed and elongated residuals in gamma-ray burst (GRB) pulse light curves. Within this model, an impactor wave within an expanding GRB jet undergoes acceleration from subluminal to superluminal velocities, or deceleration from superluminal to subluminal velocities. The impactor wave interacts with the surrounding medium, generating Cherenkov and/or other collisional radiation when exceeding the speed of light in said medium. Conversely, when traveling at speeds lower than that of light, alternative mechanisms such as thermalized Compton or synchrotron shock radiation come into play. Through these transitions, a dual set of light curve characteristics is produced via the phenomenon known as Relativistic Image Doubling (RID).

This model effectively explains various perplexing GRB pulse behaviors, encompassing the extent of elongation observed in time-reversed GRB pulse residuals and the correlation between elongation factor and pulse asymmetry. Notably, this model is universally applicable across all GRB categories, given the similarity in pulse behaviors observed in long/intermediate GRBs, short GRBs, and x-ray flares. The key parameters of this model include the impactor's Lorentz factor during subluminal motion, its Lorentz factor during superluminal motion, and the speed of light within the impacted medium.

Motivated by recent extensive experimental endeavors focused on detecting neutrinoless double-beta decays, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the scientific potential of experiments utilizing $^{76} mathrm{Ge}$. Assuming no signals, ongoing and upcoming experiments have the capability to establish a 90% lower limit on the half-life $T^{0 nu}_{1/2}  gtrsim 4 times 10^{26}~{ rm yr}$ and $T^{0 nu}_{1/2}  gtrsim 7 times 10^{27}~{ rm yr}$, respectively. The methodology for reporting evidence of neutrinoless double-beta decays is examined through the application of Bayesian statistical principles. For the first time, we provide a quantitative analysis of the experimental capacity to differentiate between normal and inverted neutrino mass orderings. By considering an exposure of $10^{4}~{ rm kg} cdot{ rm yr}$ and a background rate of $10^{-4}~{ rm counts}/({ rm keV} cdot{ rm kg} cdot{ rm yr})$, we determine that a moderate level of evidence supporting normal neutrino mass ordering (indicated by a Bayes factor ${ cal B}$ approximately $ ln({ cal B})  simeq 2.5$ or a probability around $92.3 %$ based on the Jeffreys scale) can be attained if the true value of effective neutrino mass $m^{}_{ beta beta}$ is below $0.

In linearized continuum elasticity, the elastic strain from a straight dislocation line weakens at a rate of $O(r^{-1})$, with $r$ representing the distance to the core of the defect. Research by Ehrlacher, Ortner, Shapeev (2016) reveals that the core correction due to nonlinear and discrete (atomistic) effects diminishes at a faster rate of $O(r^{-2})$. This study focuses on screw dislocations under pure anti-plane shear kinematics. We showcase that by fully utilizing crystalline symmetries and potentially applying a straightforward correction to the continuum far-field prediction, an enhanced decay of $O(r^{-p})$, where $p > 2$, for the core correction is achieved. This finding is particularly intriguing as it highlights instances where continuum elasticity offers more accurate predictions of the elastic field surrounding a dislocation than anticipated. It also holds significance for atomistic simulation of dislocation cores, which we further elaborate on.

The impact of internal adaptation dynamics on the self-organized aggregation of chemotactic bacteria was examined through Monte Carlo (MC) simulations utilizing a two-stream kinetic transport equation coupled with a reaction-diffusion equation for the chemoattractant produced by the bacteria. An interesting discovery was the nonmonotonic trend in peak aggregation density concerning adaptation time. Specifically, aggregation was most pronounced when the adaptation time closely matched or slightly exceeded the average bacteria run time. Furthermore, a peculiar observation was the emergence of a trapezoidal aggregation profile at significantly longer adaptation times. This led to constrained motion of individual cells during plateau phases due to limitations in tumbling frequency modulation.

Additionally, an asymptotic analysis of the kinetic transport system was conducted, resulting in a novel asymptotic equation for large adaptation times, while Keller-Segel type equations were derived for moderate adaptation times. A numerical comparison between the asymptotic equations and MC results revealed that the trapezoidal aggregation pattern was accurately captured by the novel asymptotic equation. The nonmonotonic trend in peak aggregation density was attributed to the transitional nature of asymptotic solutions across varying adaptation time intervals.

In the study of isotropic solids and fluids under imposed volume or pressure conditions, we analyze the correlations between instantaneous pressure and its ideal and excess components. Emphasizing the compression modulus K, it is highlighted that the stress fluctuation representation of elastic moduli can be obtained directly by comparing stress fluctuations in conjugate ensembles, without the need for a microscopic displacement field. This is demonstrated through the computation of the Rowlinson stress fluctuation expression K_row for NPT ensembles. The relationship K_row|P = P_id (2 - P_id/K) is established theoretically and numerically, where P_id represents the ideal pressure contribution.

In our research, we analyze the ferromagnetic Ising model incorporating long-range interactions within a two-dimensional framework. Initial findings from a Monte Carlo investigation reveal the prevalence of long-range interactions compared to short-range counterparts within the intermediate interaction range. Through a thorough examination using renormalization group techniques, we introduce a method to quantify the impact of long-range interactions through dimensional adjustments.

This paper addresses the challenge of rendering novel views of human performers wearing clothes with intricate texture patterns using a sparse set of camera views. While some recent studies have achieved impressive rendering quality on humans with uniform textures using sparse views, rendering quality remains limited when dealing with complex texture patterns due to the inability to recover high-frequency geometry details observed in the input views. 

To overcome this limitation, we introduce HDhuman, a method that combines a human reconstruction network with a pixel-aligned spatial transformer and a rendering network with geometry-guided pixel-wise feature integration to achieve high-quality human reconstruction and rendering. The pixel-aligned spatial transformer calculates correlations between input views to generate human reconstruction results with high-frequency details. This information guides multi-view feature integration through geometry-guided pixel-wise visibility reasoning, allowing the rendering network to produce high-quality images at 2k resolution for novel views. 

Unlike previous neural rendering approaches that require training or fine-tuning independent networks for different scenes, our method is a general framework that can be applied to novel subjects. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses prior generic or specific methods in both synthetic and real-world data scenarios.

A search for the rare decays $B^0_s \rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $B^0 \rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^-$ was conducted by the LHCb experiment using 1.1 fb$^{-1}$ of data at $\sqrt{s}=8$ TeV and 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ of data at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. An excess of $B^0_s \rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^-$ candidates compared to background expectations was observed with a statistical significance of 3.5 standard deviations. The branching fraction of $B^0_s \rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^- = (3.2^{+1.5}_{-1.2}) \times 10^{-9}$ was determined through an unbinned maximum likelihood fit, which aligns with the Standard Model prediction. The number of observed $B^0 \rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^-$ candidates was consistent with background expectations, yielding an upper limit on the branching fraction of $B^0 \rightarrow \mu^+ \mu^- < 9.4 \times 10^{-10}$.

We ascertain the phase diagram of the Abelian-Higgs model in one spatial dimension and time (1+1D) on a lattice. Within this analysis, we delineate a line where first-order phase transitions occur, acting as a boundary between the Higgs region and the confined region. This delineated line concludes at a quantum critical point, beyond which a smooth crossover connects the two regions. Upon scrutinizing the critical point, we unearth compelling evidence supporting its characterization as the amalgamation of two non-interacting systems: a massless free fermion and a massless free boson. Nonetheless, our exploration also reveals unexpected outcomes that defy explanation within our simplistic framework, hinting at the possibility of this newly discovered critical point being an atypical phenomenon.

We investigate the non-equilibrium dynamics of a uniform quantum Ising ring following a sudden change in the transverse field $g$ from zero to a non-zero value, known as a quench. Utilizing a Pfaffian method recently developed by N. Wu (Phys. Rev. E 101, 042108, 2020), we precisely determine the long-term reduced dynamics of a single spin and two nearest-neighbor spins in finite but large rings. 

We conduct numerical analyses on various properties including the time evolution of transverse and longitudinal magnetizations, single-spin purity, the expectation value of the string operator $X_j= \prod^{j-1}_{l=1} \sigma^z_l \sigma^x_j$, equal-time two-site correlators, and pairwise concurrence after different phase quenches. Key findings include: (i) Generic odd operators tend towards zero in the long run; (ii) The time dependence of $ \langle X_j \rangle_t$ shows exponential decay independent of $j$ following a quench to $g=1$, with the time to reach its initial peak scaling linearly with $j$; (iii) Dynamics of single-spin purity are predominantly influenced by $ \langle \sigma^x_j \rangle_t$ ($ \langle \sigma^z_j \rangle_t$) for quenches to $g<1$ ($g \geq 1$).
