We conduct the initial cosmological assessment of an enhanced cluster catalog sourced from the Red-Sequence Cluster Survey (RCS). The dataset comprises 956 clusters within the redshift range of 0.35 to 0.95, selected based on cluster richness and its associated error. Spanning 72.07 square degrees of imaging data, the calibration of the survey images has been rigorously validated against data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Employing a self-calibration method encompassing scatter in the mass-richness relationship, we simultaneously determine Omega_M and sigma_8, along with four parameters characterizing the calibration of cluster richness to mass, its redshift-dependent evolution, and scatter within the richness-mass connection. The primary aim of this comprehensive analysis is to ascertain the consistency between the derived parameters (both cosmological and cluster mass-related) and existing findings from independent sources. The unconstrained assessment yields values of 0.31+0.11-0.10 for Omega_M and 0.67+0.18-0.13 for sigma_8, while incorporating Gaussian priors on the mass-richness relation results in very similar estimates: 0.30+0.12-0.11 for Omega_M and 0.70+0.27-0.15 for sigma_8. Both analyses align well with current scientific literature. The parameters describing the mass-richness relationship in the unconstrained model are deemed reasonable and consistent with supplementary data from both RCS-1 and other cluster datasets. Our findings underscore the potential for forthcoming surveys, encompassing larger cluster samples across various wavelengths, to provide cosmological constraints that rival those obtained through alternate methods.

Human pose estimation (HPE) plays a crucial role in the development of AI-based context-aware systems within the operating room (OR). Despite the continuous use of images from OR ceiling-mounted cameras, privacy concerns may arise, even when utilizing depth images from RGB-D sensors. Utilizing low-resolution privacy-preserving images exclusively could address these concerns and facilitate the expansion of computer-assisted approaches relying on such data across multiple ORs. This study introduces the challenge of HPE on low-resolution depth images and presents a comprehensive solution that combines a multi-scale super-resolution network with a 2D human pose estimation network. By leveraging intermediate feature-maps produced at different super-resolution levels, our approach achieves accurate body pose results on low-resolution images measuring 64x48, comparable to those obtained through training and testing on full resolution images sized at 640x480.

The layered transition-metal Borides $A$B$_2$ ($A =$ Os, Ru) exhibit a structural arrangement characterized by alternating $T$ and B layers, with the B layers forming a puckered honeycomb pattern. Our study focuses on investigating the superconducting properties of RuB$_2$, which displays a critical temperature $T_c  approx 1.5$K. This investigation involves conducting measurements of the magnetic susceptibility as a function of temperature $T$, magnetization as a function of magnetic field $H$, resistivity as a function of temperature $T$, and heat capacity as a function of temperature $T$ under various magnetic field strengths $H$. 

A notable observation is the diminished heat capacity anomaly at $T_c$, indicated by $ Delta C/ gamma T_c  approx 1.1$, suggesting the presence of multi-gap superconductivity. Strong evidence supporting this notion arises from successful fitting of the electronic specific heat data to a two-gap model, with gap values $ Delta_1/k_BT_c  approx 1.88$ and $ Delta_2/k_BT_c  approx 1.13$. Furthermore, analysis of magnetization versus magnetic field measurements reveals characteristics consistent with Type-I superconductivity, corroborated by estimates of the Ginzburg-Landau parameter $ kappa  approx 0.1$--$0.66$. Collectively, these findings strongly indicate the presence of multi-gap Type-I superconductivity in RuB$_2.

Additionally, computational assessments were conducted to determine the band structure and Fermi surface of RuB$_2. The Fermi surface comprises one quasi-two-dimensional sheet and two nested ellipsoidal sheets closely resembling Os

Tactile perception plays a crucial role in real-world manipulation tasks, but the high cost and fragility of tactile sensors can hinder their practicality. This study delves into BeadSight, an inexpensive, open-source tactile sensor, in conjunction with a tactile pre-training approach as an alternative to precise, pre-calibrated sensors. The goal is to boost robustness and cut costs in manipulation systems by pre-training with the tactile sensor and then deactivating it during subsequent tasks. The focus is on determining whether tactile pre-training, even with a less accurate sensor like BeadSight, can enhance the performance of an imitation learning agent on intricate manipulation tasks. By conducting visuo-tactile pre-training on both similar and dissimilar tasks, the study examines its impact on a more extended downstream task. Results from experiments reveal that visuo-tactile pre-training led to performance improvements of up to 65% on a USB cable plugging task with vision-only inference. Furthermore, across different versions of a longer-horizon drawer pick-and-place task, pre-training consistently resulted in enhanced performance, underscoring the potential for a large-scale visuo-tactile pre-trained encoder.

The models of Multi-arm bandit (MAB) and Stochastic linear bandit (SLB) hold significance in the realm of reinforcement learning. It is widely acknowledged that traditional algorithms for bandits with a time horizon of $T$ exhibit a regret of $ Omega( sqrt{T})$. This study delves into MAB and SLB incorporating quantum reward oracles, presenting quantum algorithms for both models with regret complexities of $O( mbox{poly}( log T))$, thereby significantly enhancing the efficiency in relation to $T$. To our knowledge, this marks the inaugural demonstration of a verifiable quantum acceleration in regrets concerning bandit issues and exploitation within reinforcement learning. In contrast to previous works on quantum exploration algorithms for MAB and reinforcement learning, our approach adopts a more straightforward quantum input model, operating solely on quantum oracles allocated to individual arms.

We offer a geometric interpretation of the annihilation range in reactions involving $ \bar{p}p \rightarrow$ {two light mesons}, which is influenced by Lorentz effects in highly relativistic final states ($\gamma = E_{\mathrm{cm}}/2mc^2 \approx 6.8-8.0$). By considering Lorentz-boosted meson wave functions within the constituent quark model framework, we observe a more complex angular dependence in the annihilation amplitudes, leading to increased contributions from higher partial waves ($J>1) compared to conventional results. This approach provides insight into the nature of the short annihilation range and its relationship with the angular distribution of final states.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) enables the imaging of entire star cluster populations in galaxies at significant cosmological redshifts. This requires the application of K-corrections to their magnitudes and color indices. Star clusters typically have homogeneous stellar populations in terms of age and metallicity, leading to distinct spectral energy distributions compared to galaxies or supernovae, resulting in unique K-corrections. We present photometric K-corrections as a function of redshift for model star clusters with diverse ages and metallicities, focusing on broadband filters used by HST/ACS and JWST/NIRCam for imaging star clusters in distant galaxies. Additionally, we introduce a user-friendly webtool called RESCUER in the Appendix, which can generate K-values based on customized cluster properties.

This study focuses on exploring the direct limits of finite-dimensional basic classical simple Lie superalgebras. Additionally, we analyze the conjugacy classes of Cartan subalgebras within the group of automorphisms.

In the field of 3D human pose estimation, the traditional method involves predicting body joint coordinates based on the hip position. While effective for single individuals, this approach falls short when dealing with multiple interacting people. To address this limitation, recent methods have emerged that first estimate a root-relative pose and then calculate translation through a secondary optimization task. Our proposed neural network takes a different approach by predicting joints in a camera-centered coordinate system rather than root-relative coordinates. This unique feature allows our network to operate in a single step without requiring post-processing. As a result, our network outperforms previous methods on the MuPoTS-3D dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results.
In this study, we establish a condition for $(\alpha, \beta)$-metrics where isotropic S-curvature, weakly isotropic S-curvature, and isotropic mean Berwald curvature are shown to be equivalent.

Numerous algorithms for detecting ellipses have been developed and extensively researched over the years; however, the challenge of accurately and efficiently detecting ellipses in real-world images persists. This paper introduces an industry-focused ellipse detector based on arc-support line segments, which achieves high levels of accuracy and efficiency simultaneously. By extracting arc-support line segments to simplify complex curves in images while preserving key properties such as convexity and polarity, successful ellipse detection is facilitated. The formation of arc-support groups involves robustly linking line segments believed to be part of the same ellipse, leading to the identification of ellipses. Subsequently, two approaches are employed - locally selecting the most salient arc-support group and globally searching all valid paired groups - to quickly fit initial ellipses. Hierarchical clustering of the 5D parameter space of initial ellipses is used to generate an ellipse candidate set. The final step involves selecting and refining prominent ellipse candidates as detections through rigorous verification. Extensive experiments conducted on three public datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of F-measure scores. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/AlanLuSun/High-quality-ellipse-detection.

We introduce the initial optimal power spectrum estimation and three-dimensional deprojections for both dark and luminous matter, along with their cross correlations. These outcomes are achieved through the utilization of a novel optimal fast estimator (Pen 2003), deprojected via minimum variance and SVD techniques. The study showcases the resulting 3-D power spectra for dark matter and galaxies, in addition to their covariance pertaining to the VIRMOS-DESCART weak lensing shear and galaxy data. The survey demonstrates its highest sensitivity towards nonlinear scales denoted as k_NL ~ 1 h Mpc^-1. Notably, our 3-D power spectrum of dark matter at these scales shows notable alignment with the RCS 3-D power spectrum identified by Hoekstra et al in 2002. Furthermore, our galaxy power closely resembles that of the 2MASS survey, surpassing that of SDSS, APM, and RCS, which is consistent with anticipated discrepancies in galaxy populations.

For the I selected galaxies, we ascertain an average bias of b=1.24+/-0.18, alongside a cross-correlation coefficient of r=0.75+/-0.23. These findings, combined with the power spectra, comprehensively encapsulate the complete two-point information concerning dark matter and galaxies, encompassing galaxy-galaxy lensing effects. We also delve into the implications concerning galaxy halos and mass-to-light ratios. The most suitable "halo" parameter h=r/b=0.57+/-0.16 suggests that dynamical mass assessments based on galaxies systematically underestimate total mass.

Looking ahead, ongoing surveys like the Canada-France-Hawaii-Telescope-Legacy survey are poised to substantially enhance the dynamic range, while future photometric redshift catalogs will enable tomography following similar principles.

Coaches play a crucial role in fostering effective collaboration, yet constraints related to costs and resources often restrict their availability during real-world tasks. This limitation presents significant challenges in critical areas like healthcare and disaster response, where successful teamwork is essential. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel approach utilizing artificial intelligence (AI): task-time team coaching. Our solution, Socratic, functions as an AI system that works alongside human coaches by offering real-time guidance throughout task execution. Socratic monitors team dynamics, identifies discrepancies in team members' mutual comprehension, and provides automated interventions to optimize team performance. Through two human subject experiments focused on dyadic collaboration, we have validated the effectiveness of Socratic. The outcomes highlight that the system notably improves team performance with minimal interventions. Participants also view Socratic as a valuable and reliable tool, indicating its potential for widespread adoption. These findings suggest promising avenues for both AI research and practical implementations aimed at enhancing teamwork among individuals.

Following recent updates on measurements of $R_K$ and $R_{K^*}$ by the LHCb and Belle collaborations, we investigate the potential impact of New Physics on $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions using effective field theories. Our analysis focuses on deviations from Lepton Flavour Universality in both the Weak Effective Theory and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. In the Weak Effective Theory, our findings suggest a preference for scenarios where two operators are simultaneously present: a left-handed quark current with vector muon coupling and a right-handed quark current with axial muon coupling, regardless of how hadronic uncertainties are handled. In the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, different scenarios are identified based on the treatment of hadronic effects. A more aggressive estimate of hadronic uncertainties indicates the presence of two operators - one with left-handed quark and muon couplings, and another with left-handed quark and right-handed muon couplings. Conversely, a more conservative approach to hadronic matrix elements allows for a wider range of scenarios, including those involving only the purely left-handed operator with muon coupling.

The surface morphology of Si(100) surfaces was analyzed following 1.5 MeV Sb implantation. Scanning Probe Microscopy was employed for this investigation. Nano-sized defect features were identified on the Si surfaces at different fluences. These nanostructures are elliptical in shape and increase in size with higher fluences. Additionally, a shape transition from elliptical to circular-like was observed at high fluences. The alterations in surface roughness related to Sb fluence will also be addressed.

We address the challenge of domain generalization (DG) by treating it as a domain adaptation (DA) problem. This involves creating a worst-case target domain and adjusting a model to perform well in that scenario, ultimately enhancing the model's resilience. To generate data that is both difficult yet maintains semantic meaning, we create Fourier amplitude images and merge them with phase images from the source domain. This approach leverages the common belief in signal processing that amplitude spectra primarily influence image style, while phase data captures image semantics.

In order to generate a worst-case domain for adaptation, we engage in adversarial training between the classifier and the amplitude generator. Specifically, we utilize the principle of maximum classifier discrepancy (MCD) from domain adaptation, which links target domain performance to the variation between classifiers in the model hypothesis space. Through Bayesian hypothesis modeling, we effectively represent the model hypothesis space as a posterior distribution over classifiers based on the source domains, allowing for feasible adversarial MCD minimization.

When evaluated on the DomainBed benchmark using the extensive DomainNet dataset, our proposed method demonstrates a significant enhancement in domain generalization performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

This study presents, for the first time, the impact of pentavalent substitution at the manganese site of La(0.67)Ca(0.33)MnO(3). The ferromagnetic-metallic state undergoes a transition to a cluster-glass insulator when x exceeds 0.03. Notably, the reduction in transition temperatures (39K/at.%) is the most significant among reported substitutions at the manganese site in manganites. Our findings suggest that the charge state (valence) of the substituent plays a crucial role in altering the ferromagnetic-metallic state in colossal magnetoresistance (CMR) manganites.

We present a comprehensive study of quantum correlations near a black hole focusing on measurement-induced nonlocality (MIN). The analysis considers fermionic, bosonic, and mixed fermion-boson modes in relation to Hawking radiation. Results indicate that at infinite Hawking temperatures, only fermionic correlations remain accessible. However, higher frequency modes can maintain correlations at finite Hawking temperatures, with mixed systems showing greater sensitivity to increases in fermionic frequencies compared to bosonic ones. As MIN diminishes rapidly for the latter modes, escalating frequencies may be crucial in sustaining nonlocal correlations in scenarios involving finite Hawking temperatures.

Millions of users worldwide utilize the data processing and sharing advantages offered by cloud environments, where data security and privacy are essential concerns. The widespread use and sharing of data among users can create security vulnerabilities. This paper explores the cloud environment, its benefits, challenges, and current research trends focused on ensuring secure data processing and sharing.

Quantum field theory, the foundation of particle physics, mandates adherence to $CPT$ invariance in all processes. Therefore, it is crucial to verify the conservation of $CPT$. This study demonstrates that time-dependent $CP$ asymmetries in $B$ decays to a $CP$ eigenstate provide sufficient data to assess violations of $T$ and $CPT$ in $B^0$-${ bar B}^0$ mixing, beyond the traditional weak phases that violate $CP$. The analysis can be conducted at LHCb and the $B$ factories without the need for entangled $B^0{ bar B}^0$ states, while accounting for penguin pollution, and even when there is no difference in width between $B^0$ and ${ bar B}^0$.

The reciprocity relations of the relative Fisher information (RFI) and a generalized RFI-Euler theorem are derived self-consistently from the Hellmann-Feynman theorem. These novel reciprocity relations expand upon the RFI-Euler theorem and form the foundation for constructing a mathematical Legendre transform structure (LTS) similar to that in thermodynamics, which underpins the RFI framework. This showcases the potential to transpose the entire mathematical framework of thermodynamics into a theoretical framework based on RFI. Virial theorems play a crucial role in this process, as they link a Schrödinger-like equation to the RFI. By utilizing the RFI-LTS connection and the quantum mechanical virial theorem, Lagrange multipliers are determined. Using an appropriate ansatz, probability density functions (pdf's) and energy eigenvalues for the aforementioned Schrödinger-like equation can be inferred. The energy eigenvalues obtained through inference are compared against established theoretical and numerical results. A solid theoretical foundation is laid to reconstruct the RFI framework from the FIM framework. Numerical examples for specific cases are provided as illustrations.

Probing in mixed-integer programming (MIP) involves temporarily fixing variables to reveal useful implications for branch-and-cut solvers. Traditionally, variables are fixed one at a time, but this paper introduces a novel two-column probing scheme that fixes a pair of variables simultaneously in each iteration. While this approach requires more effort per iteration compared to the one-column method, it results in stronger implied bounds and identifies more conflicts. The prototype implementation of this scheme won first prize at the MIP Workshop 2024 Computational Competition for innovative presolving techniques. In addition to presenting the serial prototype, this paper introduces an efficient parallelization strategy that utilizes hardware acceleration to enhance solve times. Although the parallel version sacrifices some strength in each pair probed, it significantly increases the total number of probings, as demonstrated in computational experiments.

The prevalence of deceptive behavior among consumers in their online reviews poses a significant challenge, casting doubt on the reliability of information used for decision-making. Drawing from my dissertation on fabricated Google reviews of eateries (Berry, 2024), this study utilizes a tool to measure people's trust levels. Analyzing a sample of n=351, it offers insights into the prevalence of dishonesty in online reviews and profiles individuals prone to falsehoods. A predictive model for identifying fake online reviews is developed, with broader implications for studying deceptive practices and misinformation dissemination. The study also explores the potential link between dishonesty and antisocial tendencies as gauged by the trust measurement tool in Berry (2024). Additionally, it outlines future research avenues and acknowledges limitations.

Utilizing the co-area formula, a precise relaxation framework is introduced for minimizing objectives involving the total variation of a binary valued function with bounded variation. This approach covers a wide range of significant applications, including binary image restoration, segmentation, minimal compliance topology optimization, optimal design of composite membranes, and more. By converting the binary constraint into a box constraint, the relaxation method demonstrates that thresholding a solution from the relaxed problem almost certainly provides a solution to the original binary-valued problem. The stability of solutions under data perturbations is analyzed, and volume constraints are taken into account for applications like structure optimization. To efficiently solve the relaxed problem numerically, a locally superlinearly convergent algorithm is proposed. This algorithm is based on an exact penalization technique, Fenchel duality, and a semismooth Newton approach. The paper concludes with a discussion on numerical results for various applications, particularly in mathematical image processing.

The unknown isotope 26S, which is anticipated to undergo decay through two-proton (2p) emission, was investigated both theoretically and experimentally. The nucleus's structure was analyzed using the relativistic mean field (RMF) method. A technique was developed to consider the many-body structure in three-body decay calculations. The RMF results were utilized as input for the three-cluster decay model, which was employed to explore a potential 2p decay pathway for this isotope. Experimental efforts to detect 26S were carried out by initiating fragmentation reactions with a 50.3 A MeV 32S beam. Unfortunately, no occurrences of 26S or 25P (a subset of 26S believed to be proton-unstable) were detected. Based on the production systematics obtained, an upper limit for the half-life of T_{1/2}<79 ns was determined using time-of-flight measurements via the fragment separator. Combining this with theoretical estimates for the lifetime of two-proton decay yielded a decay energy threshold of Q_{2p}>640 keV for 26S. Corresponding limits for 25P were determined as T_{1/2}<38 ns and Q_{p}>110 keV. If one-proton emission is the primary decay mode for 26S, a constraint of Q_{2p}>230 keV would apply to this isotope. It is probable that 26S has a lifetime in the picosecond range, making further exploration of this isotope promising using the decay-in-flight technique.

We classify third-order integrable systems of evolution equations based on higher symmetries. By focusing on polynomial systems that are 0-homogeneous when variables are weighted appropriately with the main matrix $***$ exhibiting seventh-order symmetry, we uncover a new integrable equation. We provide the Lax representation and bi-Hamiltonian structures for this newly discovered supersymmetric equation.

We present a nonstationary spatio-temporal statistical model for gridded data on the sphere that specifies a computationally convenient covariance structure dependent on varying geography. Traditional statistical models on a spherical domain are nonstationary across latitudes, but stationary at the same latitude (axial symmetry). This assumption is considered too limiting for variables like surface temperature, impacted by broad geographical factors such as land and ocean. Our proposed evolutionary spectrum approach accommodates diverse regimes across Earth's geography, leading to a more general and flexible model class that outperforms axially symmetric models significantly. It captures longitudinal patterns that would otherwise be assumed constant. The model is estimated using a multi-step conditional likelihood approximation that maintains nonstationary features while enabling distributed computations. We demonstrate that fitting data sets exceeding 20 million records can be accomplished in under a day using cutting-edge workstations. Once parameters are estimated, surrogate runs can be instantly generated from a standard laptop. Additionally, the statistical model's resulting estimates serve as a synthetic summary of the space-time characteristics of an entire initial condition ensemble, offering superior compression rates compared to traditional bit-by-bit compression algorithms used in climate modeling.

We present a novel demonstration of the distinctiveness of solutions to the Gross-Pitaevskii hierarchy, initially proven by Erdos, Schlein, and Yau. Our approach involves a different spatial framework and relies on space-time estimates.

Quantum critical scaling in a magnetic field near saturation is illustrated for a CuPzN compound with an $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain. This is achieved by analyzing previously published data on magnetization, thermal expansion, and NMR relaxation. The magnetization scaling is evidenced by consolidating data across various temperatures and fields onto a unified curve without relying on any theoretical assumptions. The resulting data collapse aligns closely with the theoretically projected scaling function, devoid of any adjustable parameters. The quantum critical region's experimental boundaries are delineated by the deviation of scaled data from the theoretical function beyond a certain range. Notably, the thermal expansion also exhibits quantum critical scaling akin to magnetization. Moreover, the NMR relaxation rate $1/T_1$ near saturation adheres to the expected quantum critical behavior of $1/T_1 \propto T^{-0.5}$ up to temperatures around $k_{\mathrm{B}}T \approx J$, where $J$ represents the exchange coupling constant.

Conventional methods of screening for anxiety and depression present obstacles to effectively monitoring and treating these conditions. Nevertheless, recent advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP) and speech modeling enable the integration of textual, acoustic, and manually crafted language-based features to lay the groundwork for future mental health screening and condition detection. Speech serves as a valuable and easily accessible resource for gaining insights into an individual's cognitive state. By harnessing various facets of speech, novel digital biomarkers for depression and anxiety can be developed. In this context, we advocate for a multi-modal system designed for screening depression and anxiety through self-administered speech tasks. The proposed framework combines deep-learned features extracted from audio and text with manually crafted features guided by clinically validated domain expertise. Our research indicates that enhancing manually crafted features with deep-learned features enhances the overall classification F1 score from 0.58 to 0.63 for depression and from 0.54 to 0.57 for anxiety compared to a baseline solely reliant on manually crafted features. These findings underscore the potential of speech-based biomarkers in shaping the future landscape of digital health.

String theory is a leading contender as a primary quantum theory encompassing all interactions, including Einstein gravity. Within string theory, certain solutions can be understood as black holes. By employing both the semi-analytic and WKB methods, researchers have examined the quasinormal modes (QNMs) of 1+1 dimensional black holes in string theory. Additionally, numerical methods were used to calculate the QNMs of 1+3 dimensional black holes in string theory. These numerical findings indicate that specific QNMs play a dominant role in governing the late-time gravitational oscillations of black holes subjected to external perturbations.

Our research focuses on analyzing the characteristics of optimal trajectories for particles moving on a two-dimensional surface comprised of distinct regions. These particles travel at constant speeds varying between regions and along region boundaries. Notably, particle velocity peaks when moving along the boundaries between two regions, exhibiting a behavior similar to Snell's Law in optics but with broader applications. This model can be utilized to investigate animal and insect paths that frequently align along edges. Three distinct trajectory behaviors near corner edges are predicted by the model: complete edge-following, partial edge-following, and total avoidance of the edge, mirroring observations in natural ant trails.

This study introduces a dataset comprising one thousand passive spiral galaxies at redshift $z=$ 0.01-0.3, obtained through an integrated analysis of the Third Public Data Release of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP PDR3) and the GALEX-SDSS-WISE Legacy Catalog (GSWLC-2). From a dataset of 54,871 $gri$ galaxy images extracted from the HSC-SSP PDR3 covering an area of 1072 deg$^2$, a search was conducted using deep-learning morphological classification to identify passive spiral candidates falling below the star-forming main sequence as determined by UV to mid-IR SED fitting in the GSWLC-2. Subsequently, these candidates were categorized into 1100 passive spirals and 1141 secondary samples following visual inspections. The majority of the secondary samples are identified as passive ringed S0 or pseudo-ringed galaxies, while the remaining cases exhibit uncertain morphologies, including two peculiar objects characterized by diamond-shaped stellar features. The selected passive spirals exhibit a distribution similar to that of typical quiescent galaxies on the EW$_ mathrm{H delta}$-D$_n$4000 diagram and concentration indices. Furthermore, an increased proportion of passive spiral galaxies was observed in X-ray clusters. Within galaxy clusters, passive spiral galaxies tend to be situated in the intermediate or late infall phases on the phase-space diagram, lending support to the ram pressure scenario frequently proposed in previous research. The dataset and composite $gri$ images can be accessed on the HSC-SSP PDR3 website (https://hsc.mtk.nao.ac.jp/ssp/data-release/). Future enhancements, such as integration with a citizen science initiative dedicated to HSC data, aim to facilitate more efficient and comprehensive classifications.

In Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) with $N_c$ colors, the anti-symmetric valence quark color space singlet state $ \sim  \epsilon_{i_1 \cdots i_{N_c}} |i_1, \cdots, i_{N_c} \rangle$ representing the proton corresponds to a reduced density matrix $ \rho_{ij}=(1/N_c)  \delta_{ij}$ for a single color degree of freedom. The degenerate spectrum of eigenvalues, $ \lambda_i=1/N_c$, purity $ \mathrm{tr}~ \rho^2 = 1/N_c$, and von Neumann entropy $S_{\mathrm{vN}}= \log(N_c)$ collectively indicate maximal color entanglement. Conversely, in the limit as $N_c$ approaches infinity, the spatial wave function of the proton decomposes into valence quark wave functions governed by a mean field (E. Witten, Nucl. Phys. B 160 (1979) p. 57), devoid of spatial entanglement. A model calculation at $N_c=3$ employing a basic three quark model light-front wave function by Brodsky and Schlumpf predicts entanglement at the percent level in spatial degrees of freedom. Through light-cone perturbation theory, we deduce the density matrix linked to the four parton $|qqqg \rangle$ Fock state. By tracing out the quarks, we construct the reduced density matrix for the gluon's degrees of freedom, capturing its entanglement with the sources. Our formulas reveal the density matrix's reliance on the soft cutoff $x$ for the gluon's light-cone momentum, along with collinear and ultraviolet regulators. The importance of studying asymptotically flat spaces in loop quantum gravity is discussed, followed by a review of extending the standard framework to this sector using the GNS construction. A procedure for creating new Hilbert spaces for loop quantum gravity on non-compact spatial manifolds is outlined. These Hilbert spaces represent fluctuations around fixed backgrounds and can be interpreted as states. Choosing backgrounds that approximate classical asymptotically flat 3-geometries provides a natural framework for discussing physical applications of loop quantum gravity, especially its semi-classical limit. Three general proposals for constructing suitable backgrounds are presented, including an approach that can lead to quantum gravity on anti-DeSitter space as described by the Chern-Simons state.

The utilization of AI-powered computer vision systems to identify human emotions, particularly when individuals are wearing face masks, poses a novel challenge in the current Covid-19 pandemic landscape. This research introduces a facial emotion recognition system designed to detect emotions from individuals donning various face mask types. A unique data augmentation technique was applied to enhance the model's performance by incorporating four different mask variations for each facial image. The study assessed the efficacy of four convolutional neural networks – Alexnet, Squeezenet, Resnet50, and VGGFace2 – trained via transfer learning. Results from the experiments indicated that our model performed notably well in multi-mask scenarios compared to single-mask scenarios, with the VGGFace2 network achieving the highest accuracy rate of 97.82% for person-dependent mode and 74.21% for person-independent mode based on the JAFFE dataset. However, when evaluated using the UIBVFED dataset, the Resnet50 network exhibited superior performance, boasting accuracies of 73.68% for person-dependent mode and 59.57% for person-independent mode. Furthermore, various metrics including precision, sensitivity, specificity, AUC, F1 score, and confusion matrix were leveraged to comprehensively evaluate the system's efficiency. Additionally, the LIME algorithm was implemented to visually represent the decision-making process of the CNN model.

Modern software systems are highly configurable to meet various stakeholder requirements. Understanding the relationship between configurations and performance attributes is crucial for controlling and optimizing the system. However, this has been a challenging area due to the opaque nature of the system. Previous performance analyses of these systems have treated configurations as individual data points without considering their spatial relationships, limiting their ability to explore aspects like local optima. In this study, we propose a new approach to performance analysis by viewing the configuration space as a structured "landscape". To support this idea, we developed an open-source fitness landscape analysis (FLA) framework using graph data mining techniques. By applying this framework to 86 million benchmarked configurations from 32 running workloads of 3 real-world systems, we identified 6 key findings that provide a comprehensive understanding of the landscape topography and its implications for configuration tuning and performance modeling.

We present a 1.4 W continuous wavelength (CW) laser operating at 243.1 nm. This laser is created by quadrupling the frequency of a ytterbium-doped fiber amplifier system that produces over 10 W of CW power at 972.5 nm. To ensure precise frequency control, we lock the laser to an optical frequency comb and stimulate the 1S-2S transition in atomic hydrogen. This deep-UV laser, stabilized in frequency and high in power, is highly valuable for accurate spectroscopy of both common and rare atoms, hydrogen two-photon laser cooling, and Raman spectroscopy.

The fields of autonomous systems and robotics are gaining significant attention in civil applications like construction, logistics, and firefighting. However, the widespread use of these technologies is impeded by the need for robust processing units to operate AI models. Edge-AI solutions show great potential, enabling efficient and cost-effective robotics that can automate civil services, enhance safety, and promote sustainability. This study introduces an innovative Edge-AI-enabled drone-based surveillance system for autonomous multi-robot operations in construction sites. Our system incorporates a lightweight MCU-based object detection model into a custom UAV platform with a 5G-enabled multi-agent coordination framework. Our focus is on real-time obstacle detection and dynamic path planning in construction settings, providing a tailored dataset for MCU-based edge applications. Through field experiments, we demonstrate practical feasibility and determine optimal operational parameters, showcasing the scalability and computational efficiency advantages of our approach over existing UAV solutions. We also discuss the current and future roles of autonomous vehicles on construction sites and the efficacy of edge-AI solutions. Our dataset is publicly available at github.com/egirgin/storaige-b950.

Utilizing laser cooling on weak transitions is an effective method to achieve ultracold temperatures in atoms with multiple valence electrons. However, strongly magnetic atoms pose a challenge as the traditional narrow-line magneto-optical trap (MOT) faces destabilization due to the conflicting optical and magnetic forces. To address this issue with Erbium (Er) atoms, we have devised a unique narrow-line MOT that effectively balances these forces by utilizing laser light adjusted to the blue side of a narrow transition with a frequency of 8 kHz. This approach results in a spin-polarized trap population with temperatures dropping below 2 microkelvin. Our findings offer an innovative alternative for laser cooling on weak transitions, particularly suitable for rare-earth-metal and metastable alkaline earth elements.

Let $ \sigma(x)$ represent the sum of divisors of $x$. If $N$ is an odd number and $ \sigma(N) = 2N$, then an odd perfect number $N$ is considered to be in Eulerian form when it can be expressed as $N = {q^k}{n^2}$, where $q$ is a prime number satisfying $q \equiv k \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ and $ \gcd(q,n) = 1$. This study demonstrates that if $q < n$, Descartes's conjecture (previously known as Sorli's conjecture), which states $k =  \nu_{q}(N) = 1$, is invalid. Consequently, this provides an unequivocal proof for the equivalence $$k =  \nu_{q}(N) = 1  \Longleftrightarrow n < q.$$ Furthermore, building on recent findings by Cohen and Sorli, it is established that when $q < n$, either $q > 5$ or $k > 5$ must hold true. Equational Unification, a crucial issue in various fields like automated theorem proving and security protocol analysis, is the main focus of this paper. Specifically, we delve into XOR-Unification, which involves unification modulo the exclusive-or theory. This theory encompasses an operator characterized by Associativity, Commutativity, Nilpotency, and the existence of an identity element. Within the Coq proof assistant, we have developed an algorithm based on Liu and Lynch's work to address XOR unification problems. Through rigorous verification, we have established its soundness, completeness, and termination. Leveraging Coq's code extraction feature, we have translated this algorithm into the OCaml programming language for practical implementation.

How does the presence of missing data impact our capacity to grasp signal structures? Research indicates that the ability to learn signal structure through principal components is reliant on the balance between sample size and dimensionality, with a critical number of observations required to initiate learning (Biehl and Mietzner, 1993). This analysis is now expanded to encompass missing data. Probabilistic principal component analysis is commonly utilized to estimate signal structures in datasets containing missing data. Our analysis indicates that missing data effectively diminishes the signal-to-noise ratio, rather than reducing sample size as commonly believed. The theory anticipates a shift in learning patterns, which is corroborated by both simulated and real dataset findings.

Angular distributions of target and double spin asymmetries for the Delta(1232) in the exclusive channel (polarized-proton polarized-electron, electron-prime proton)pi0 were measured at Jefferson Lab within the Q2 range of 0.5 to 1.5 GeV^2. The obtained asymmetry results were analyzed in comparison with the unitary isobar model, dynamical models, and effective Lagrangian theory. The study revealed a notable sensitivity to various models, especially concerning the accurate depiction of background terms crucial for determining the target asymmetry.

Diffusion-driven processes play a crucial role in materials science, particularly in the realm of energy conversion and transmission. When converting chemical energy to electrical energy, the diffusion of species directly impacts the rate of exchange and, consequently, the performance of the conversion device. Similarly, as an electric field traverses a medium, it causes species to diffuse. This diffusion can be controlled to manipulate surface nano-patterns, or if left unregulated, it may result in irreversible degradation of metallic conductors. Therefore, comprehending how materials behave under the influence of diffusional species is of paramount importance in scientific research.

This dissertation aims to investigate two specific instances of species diffusion in energy conversion and transmission scenarios. The primary focus is on the insertion of lithium into the cathode electrode of lithium-ion batteries and the evolution of inclusions as they propagate under electromigration in metallic conductors. Through this study, it is demonstrated that phase-field methods effectively capture the fundamental physics underlying diffusion-driven phenomena discussed herein.

In this paper, we introduce a novel learning approach for computer vision and medical imaging challenges that involve large-scale datasets containing millions of observations and features. Our method involves gradually reducing the number of variables by enforcing a sparsity constraint based on a specific criterion and schedule. The iterative reduction of the problem size makes our approach particularly suitable for handling big data learning tasks. Our technique can be applied to optimize any differentiable loss function, making it useful for regression, classification, and ranking problems. The resulting algorithms incorporate variable screening into the estimation process and are straightforward to implement. We offer theoretical assurances regarding convergence and selection consistency.

To address nonlinearity, our approach utilizes one-dimensional piecewise linear response functions, while a second-order prior is imposed on these functions to prevent overfitting. Experimental results on both real and synthetic data demonstrate that our method performs favorably compared to other advanced techniques in regression, classification, and ranking tasks. Moreover, our method is highly efficient and scalable in terms of computational resources.

In this study, we contrast nuclear forces derived from chiral effective field theory (EFT) with those from traditional models based on phenomenological and meson theories. Through a thorough comparison, we demonstrate that chiral EFT surpasses previous approaches in terms of both theoretical structure and practical utilization in ab initio computations. Despite the significant advancements facilitated by chiral EFT, unresolved issues, particularly the renormalization problem, must be addressed before complete confidence can be established.

Model selection criteria are guidelines utilized to choose the optimal statistical model from a pool of potential models, balancing accuracy and complexity. Traditionally, popular model selection criteria evaluate accuracy through the model log-likelihood function, which may lack robustness. This study introduces a novel set of robust model selection criteria for independently but not identically distributed observations (i.n.i.d.o.), based on R'enyi's pseudodistance (RP). The RP-driven model selection criterion is parameterized by $ alpha$, regulating the equilibrium between efficiency and robustness. The paper establishes theoretical foundations for the RP criterion and applies it to the context of multiple linear regression, yielding explicit expressions for the model selection criterion. Additionally, it examines restricted models and provides explicit expressions for nested models within the multiple linear regression framework. Lastly, an empirical simulation study demonstrates the method's robustness advantages.

Our research focuses on the birational boundedness of Fano varieties and Fano fibrations. By examining conjectures concerning the boundedness of these entities, we make progress towards establishing the birational boundedness of Fano fibrations through an inductive approach. This leads to the development of strategies for achieving birational boundedness and bounding the anti-canonical volumes of varieties classified as $ epsilon$-Fano type. Additionally, we demonstrate the birational boundedness of $3$-folds falling under the $ epsilon$-Fano type category.

In 1967, Kadison posed the question of whether a subfactor $N$ of a factor $M$, where $N' \cap M$ consists only of scalars, will have a maximal abelian *-subalgebra that is also maximal in $M$. Building on Popa's theorem in the type $\mathrm{II}$ case from 1981, we address Kadison's problem for all subfactors with an expectation $N \subset M$, where $N$ is either a type $\mathrm{III}_\lambda$ factor with $0 \leq \lambda < 1$, or a type $\mathrm{III}_1$ factor satisfying Connes's bicentralizer conjecture. Our solution is rooted in a novel formula for the bicentralizer algebras of various inclusions, leading to a type $\mathrm{III}$ version of Popa's local quantization principle. Expanding on Haaegrup's 1984 theorem, we establish a link between the relative bicentralizer conjecture and the Dixmier property. Furthermore, we demonstrate the validity of this conjecture for an extensive range of inclusions and prove an ergodicity theorem for the bicentralizer flow. Additionally, we apply our methods to $\mathrm{II}_1$ factors, presenting a fresh characterization of Ozawa's W*-Akemann-Ostrand property.

The study focuses on the physics of vortex lines in dipolar condensates, emphasizing the influence of the nonlocal nature of dipolar interactions. In dipolar gases, the 3D nature of vortices is more crucial compared to short-range interacting systems. The stability of transverse modes of vortex lines is significantly impacted by the dipolar interaction. Interestingly, the presence of a periodic potential along the vortex line can lead to the development of a roton minimum in the spectrum of transverse modes. We explore the specific conditions under which this roton minimum may cause instability in the straight vortex line, presenting novel possibilities for vortices in dipolar gases.

Individuals diagnosed with Type I Diabetes (T1D) are required to administer insulin injections to mitigate the adverse long-term consequences of hyperglycemia, characterized by elevated blood glucose levels (BG). It is crucial for patients to exercise caution in administering the correct dosage of insulin to avoid the risk of hypoglycemia, a condition marked by low BG levels that could potentially lead to fatality. Patients adhere to a specific regimen that dictates the appropriate insulin dosage at designated intervals. The current management approaches for this condition involve continual adjustment of the patient's regimen based on the disease's progression, as documented in the patient's diabetes diary.

The primary objective of this research is to investigate the complexities associated with BG prediction through the application of various machine learning algorithms and diverse data preprocessing techniques. This study encompasses an analysis of 312 distinct combinations involving learners and preprocessed datasets, using a novel T1D dataset comprising 29,601 entries sourced from 47 diverse patients. The most precise forecasting model identified is a composite model comprising two Gaussian Process Regression models, yielding an errL1 loss of 2.70 mmol/L (48.65 mg/dl). Notably, this outcome falls short of expectations when compared to the simplistic approach of predicting the patient's average BG, which yields an errL1 of 2.91 mmol/L (52.43 mg/dl).

Evaluation metrics for each data variant/model combination are meticulously detailed, including glucose-specific indicators, revealing marginally improved outcomes with the best-performing model displaying only incremental enhancement over basic measures. These findings underscore the limitations associated with utilizing conventional diabetes diary data in generating precise BG prediction models, highlighting the potential necessity for supplementary data sources to enhance predictive accuracy.

We examine the topological categorization of one-dimensional chiral symmetric interfaces within a two-dimensional substrate. A demonstration of the validity of this classification based on Green's function is provided through explicit assessment of the topological invariant. Additionally, we establish that a comprehensive understanding of the substrate's physics, contained within the Green's function, is essential due to entanglement between in-gap modes and the substrate. This is achieved by exploring a classification framework derived from the reduced ground state projector. Our analysis reveals that mishandling this framework can result in incorrect alterations to the topological index as a consequence of entanglement-induced gap closures. To exemplify our findings, we apply them to a tight-binding model depicting a spiral magnetic interface within an s-wave superconductor.

Future cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments are poised to achieve unparalleled precision in measuring temperature fluctuations on small angular scales. These fluctuations, originating from various late-time effects such as gravitational lensing, Doppler shifting of CMB photons by moving electrons (known as the kSZ effect), and residual foregrounds, present a complex mixture. To address this, we propose a novel statistical method that effectively separates the kSZ signal from other components. Additionally, our approach allows for the decomposition of the kSZ signal into distinct redshift bins without relying on external datasets like galaxy surveys. This decomposition extends to high redshifts and offers a unique opportunity to isolate the high-redshift signal resulting from patchy reionization. By enabling future CMB experiments to make groundbreaking measurements of the reionization era with high significance and novel insights, our method holds promise for advancing the field.
