We address the issue of exponential utility indifference valuation within a simplified framework where traded and nontraded assets are uncorrelated, but the claim to be priced may depend on both. Traded asset prices adhere to a multivariate Black and Scholes model, while nontraded asset prices evolve according to generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. We establish a BSDE representation of the utility indifference price (UIP) for a broad range of non-smooth, potentially unbounded payoffs that rely on both asset classes. Our focus shifts to European claims, leveraging the Gaussian structure of the model to utilize BSDE techniques (specifically, a Malliavin-type representation theorem by Ma (2002)) to demonstrate the regularity of Z and define the UIP for discontinuous European payoffs as a viscosity solution of a suitable PDE with continuous space derivatives. The optimal hedging strategy is essentially identified as the delta hedging strategy corresponding to the UIP. Given the absence of general closed-form formulas, we also derive asymptotic expansions for prices and hedging strategies when the risk aversion parameter is small. Finally, we apply our findings to pricing and hedging power derivatives across various structural models in energy markets.

This work serves as an instructional introduction to M-theory and its maximally supersymmetric toroidal compactifications within the frameworks of 11D supergravity, type II string theory, and M(atrix) theory. U-duality is utilized as the primary tool and guiding principle for revealing the spectrum of BPS states. The review encompasses the 11D supergravity algebra, basic 1/2-BPS solutions, discussion on T-duality from an algebraic perspective in perturbative and non-perturbative sectors, and the application of these tools to analyze U-duality at the level of the effective action and BPS spectrum. Special focus is placed on Weyl and Borel generators. The study includes deriving U-duality multiplets of BPS particles and strings, U-duality invariant mass formulas for 1/2- and 1/4-BPS states in general toroidal compactifications with gauge backgrounds on skew tori, and U-duality multiplets of constraints for states preserving a specific fraction of supersymmetry. Various enigmatic states are discovered in D<=3, whose existence is suggested by T-duality and 11D Lorentz invariance. Subsequently, a transition is made to the perspective of M(atrix) theory, providing an overview of Discrete Light Cone Quantization (DLCQ) in general and specifically for M-theory. The realization of U-duality as electric-magnetic dualities of the Matrix gauge theory is discussed, along with a detailed presentation of the Matrix gauge theory BPS spectrum and the conjectured extended U-duality group within this framework.

The interpretability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) is a crucial subject within the realm of computer vision. Recent studies in this area have commonly utilized a well-established model to elucidate the internal workings of CNNs, facilitating a comprehensive understanding of these networks. This study posits that an alternative interpretation can unveil the operational mechanisms of CNNs by drawing parallels between communication systems and CNNs. By establishing a correlation between the components of these two systems and conducting experiments to validate this connection, this paper successfully illustrates the rationale behind this relationship. Furthermore, by analyzing current advancements in neural network research, we identify a fundamental link between these two tasks that aids in providing a logical explanation for these studies and guides us towards the appropriate research direction in neural networks.

An effective divisor D on a smooth, compact complex surface X is considered even if its class [D] in H^2(X, Z) can be divided by 2. Assuming that D is reduced, being even implies the presence of a double cover Y over X that is precisely branched over D. This note aims to investigate configurations of n lines, where n is less than or equal to 10, on a smooth quartic surface X included in P_3, creating an even divisor by this definition. The findings indicate that for n up to 8, there are no unforeseen occurrences (including six lines of one type and eight lines of four types). For n=10, a partial classification has been established: Every even set of ten lines on a smooth quartic surface falls into one of eleven distinct categories. Currently, the specific types that occur remain unknown. The proof of these results involves a detailed examination of various cases.

This study explores the impact of pre-marked options in question images on multimodal language models, highlighting a phenomenon where model responses are notably influenced. A structured approach was employed to investigate this phenomenon: models were initially presented with multiple-choice question images and correctly answered, followed by exposure to versions with pre-marked options. The results indicate a significant shift in model responses towards the pre-marked option, even when conflicting with their initial neutral answers. Through comprehensive evaluations, it was determined that this bias towards agreeableness is a consistent and measurable behavior observed across different model architectures. These findings underscore potential limitations in the reliability of these models when processing images with pre-marked options, prompting critical considerations regarding their use in decision-making scenarios where such visual cues may be present.

Weak-scale supersymmetry faces a challenge with fine-tuning to achieve the correct scale for electroweak symmetry breaking, especially in the minimal supersymmetric extension of the standard model (MSSM). Our proposed solution addresses this issue without requiring an extension of the MSSM at the weak scale. Superparticle masses are generated through a balanced combination of moduli and anomaly-mediated contributions, effectively lowering the messenger scale of supersymmetry breaking to the TeV range. Key components of this solution include a substantial A term for the top squarks and a minimal B term for the Higgs doublets. By limiting fine-tuning to less than 20%, we can make precise predictions about the spectrum. Gaugino masses are nearly uniform at the weak scale, ranging from 450 to 900 GeV. Squark and slepton masses follow a similar pattern, with their mass being approximately square root of 2 smaller than that of gauginos. The exception lies in the top squarks, whose masses differ from other squarks by about mt/square root of 2. The lightest Higgs boson's mass is below 120 GeV, while tan beta, the ratio of vacuum expectation values for the two Higgs doublets, exceeds 5. The lightest superparticle is a neutral Higgsino with a mass below 190 GeV, potentially serving as dark matter. The lighter top squark may have a mass below 300 GeV, which could be relevant for Run II at the Tevatron.

This paper presents measurement results for line-of-sight MIMO links operating in the millimeter wave range. The estimated condition numbers and capacities of the measured channels align well with theoretical predictions across different transmission distances and antenna configurations. Additionally, the findings indicate that orthogonal channel vectors can be identified when the spacing criterion is met, enabling spatial multiplexing and achieving high spectral efficiencies over extended distances. Conversely, spacings leading to ill-conditioned channel matrices result in significantly diminished performance.

The concept of topological entropy for formal languages is defined as the topological entropy of the smallest topological automaton that accepts it. By utilizing a characterization of this concept based on approximations of the Myhill-Nerode congruence relation, we can determine the topological entropies of specific example languages. These examples indicate that a formal language is considered simple when it has zero entropy.

Recent research has demonstrated that all established string theory models can be derived through partial fermionization, projection, and background Ansätze from the foundational, exclusively bosonic string theory. This fundamental theory has also been revealed to represent a doubled and T-dual target spacetime that is both chiral and non-commutative. It is further established in this study that this metastring theory, as it is termed, inherently incorporates mirror symmetry.

Sound waves from the early Universe, known as baryon acoustic oscillations (BAOs), are imprinted in the large-scale structure and serve as standard rulers to measure the Universe's scale. These oscillations have been observed in galaxy distributions. We propose measuring BAOs from the density field's troughs. By analyzing accurate mock halo catalogues with and without BAOs in the seed initial conditions, we find that the BAO signal is not present in the clustering of disjoint voids but is clearly detected in overlapping voids, which represent all density field troughs. We identify these troughs using Delaunay triangulation to compute empty circumsphere centers constrained by galaxies' tetrahedra. Our theoretical models, based on detailed simulated void catalogues, align well with observational data. Utilizing a large sample of luminous red galaxies from SDSS-III BOSS DR11, we report a >3 sigma BAO detection from voids in observations for the first time. Since voids are expanding nearly isotropically, their centers serve as calm areas in the Universe, offering a unique perspective on analyzing the cosmological large-scale structure through galaxy surveys.

Reward models play a critical role in the expansion of large language models (LLMs) during both training and inference phases. However, current reward models predominantly emphasize human preferences, overlooking the potential benefits of incorporating verifiable correctness signals in enhancing LLM training. This study introduces the concept of agentic reward modeling, a reward framework that integrates various verifiable correctness signals with reward models to offer more dependable rewards. To this end, we introduce a practical implementation of a reward agent, named RewardAgent, which combines human preference rewards with two key verifiable signals - factuality and instruction adherence - to deliver more reliable rewards. Through a series of extensive experiments on established reward model benchmarks and best-of-n searches during inference on real-world downstream tasks, RewardAgent consistently outperforms traditional vanilla reward models, showcasing its efficacy. Additionally, by generating training preference pairs using RewardAgent and training an LLM with the DPO objective, we achieve superior performance on a variety of NLP benchmarks compared to conventional reward models. Our codebase is openly available to facilitate further research at https://github.com/THU-KEG/Agentic-Reward-Modeling.

Recently, there has been a growing research interest in utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) for visual generation. However, most existing methods focus on transferring LLM architecture to visual generation without thoroughly exploring the fundamental differences between language and vision. This oversight can result in underutilizing the visual generation capabilities of LLMs. 

In this study, we investigate the characteristics of visual embedding space within the LLM framework and find that the correlation between visual embeddings can lead to more stable and robust generation outcomes. Introducing IAR, an Improved AutoRegressive Visual Generation Method that enhances both training efficiency and generation quality of LLM-based visual generation models.

To begin with, we introduce a Codebook Rearrangement strategy that employs a balanced k-means clustering algorithm to reorganize the visual codebook into clusters, ensuring high similarity among visual features within each cluster. By leveraging this rearranged codebook, we propose a Cluster-oriented Cross-entropy Loss that directs the model to predict the cluster where the token is situated. This method ensures that even if the model predicts the wrong token index, there is a high likelihood that the predicted token falls within the correct cluster, thereby significantly improving generation quality and robustness.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently enhances model training efficiency and performance across different scales, reducing training time by half while maintaining the same FID score from 100M to 1.4B parameters. Furthermore, our method is applicable to various LLM-based visual generation models and aligns with the scaling law, offering a promising avenue for future research in this area. The code for our method is available at: https://github.com/sjtuplayer/IAR.

The large radius exciton spectrum in an individual semiconducting single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) is explained using an elementary potential model. This model depicts the exciton as a bound state of two oppositely charged quasi-particles confined on the tube's surface. The interaction potential's parity causes the exciton states to divide into odd and even series. It is demonstrated that the binding energy of even excitons in the ground state significantly surpasses the energy gap for both bare and screened Coulomb electron-hole (e-h) potentials. The text also delves into the factors that prevent the collapse of single-electron states within isolated semiconducting SWCNTs.

The function of spin networks in gauge theories, quantum gravity, and topological quantum field theory is outlined, focusing on their interconnections. It is contended that spin networks and their extensions offer a framework that could potentially unify various perspectives on quantum gravity and quantum geometry. Consequently, a series of hypotheses are proposed regarding the structure of a prospective theory that could serve as an advancement of the non-perturbative quantization of general relativity and a non-perturbative formulation of string theory.

We establish a direct correspondence between two types of sequences: (i) exchangeable sequences of random variables with minimum or maximum infinitely divisible finite-dimensional distributions and (ii) non-negative, non-decreasing, infinitely divisible stochastic processes. The exponent measure of an exchangeable minimum infinitely divisible sequence is comprised of a simple "drift measure" and a combination of product probability measures, uniquely corresponding to the Levy measure of a non-negative, non-decreasing infinitely divisible process. This Levy measure is supported on non-negative, non-decreasing functions. In probabilistic terms, this infinitely divisible process is equivalent to the conditional cumulative hazard process linked with the exchangeable sequence of random variables featuring minimum or maximum infinitely divisible marginals. Our findings offer a comprehensive framework that encompasses various interesting classes of multivariate distributions, including exogenous shock models, exponential and geometric laws with lack-of-memory property, min-stable multivariate exponential and extreme-value distributions, as well as reciprocal Archimedean copulas with completely monotone generator and Archimedean copulas with log-completely monotone generator.

A novel calibration method for H-fs-TALIF is introduced to determine the ratio of two-photon absorption cross-sections, $ sigma^{(2)}$, for atomic hydrogen (H) and krypton (Kr) in the context of a femtosecond laser system's broadband emission. The estimated ratio of the two-photon absorption cross-sections for H and Kr is $ sigma^{(2)}$ for H and Kr $ sigma^{(2)}$(Kr)/$ sigma^{(2)}$(H) = $0.027 pm 20$%, significantly lower compared to previous values obtained using narrowband nanosecond lasers. This discrepancy underscores the necessity for independent calibration of TALIF measurements within a specific laser pulsewidth range.

Recovering images from optical interferometric observations poses a significant challenge in the field. Unlike observations at radio wavelengths, atmospheric turbulence rapidly alters phase measurements in the optical realm, leading to corruption. To address this issue, various groups have devised image reconstruction methods relying solely on squared visibility and closure phase data, which remain unaffected by atmospheric disturbances. This study showcases the outcomes of two techniques employed by our team, utilizing coherently integrated data from the Navy Prototype Optical Interferometer. Through these approaches, we successfully reconstructed complex visibilities for multiple sources and generated images using conventional radio imaging software. The techniques utilized, data corrections made, resulting images of selected sources, and the implications of these findings are detailed in this presentation.

We incorporate spherical Rindler space, which features a spherical void at its core, into asymptotically AdS spacetime. It is demonstrated that this configuration possesses a gravitational entropy proportional to the area of the void. This spherical AdS-Rindler space corresponds holographically to a section of the boundary field theory with limited time duration, restricting access to information about finite spatial regions due to the finite duration of measurements. We introduce the concept of Residual Entropy to account for the uncertainty regarding a system's state resulting from local, finite-time observations. By leveraging holography and the strong subadditivity of entanglement in two-dimensional conformal field theories, we propose a formula for Residual Entropy that accurately reflects the areas of circular voids in AdS3. Expanding this concept to field theories on strips with varying time durations, it is demonstrated that Residual Entropy effectively calculates the areas of all closed, non-uniform curves on a spatial slice of AdS3. The discussion extends to higher-dimensional field theories, highlighting the relationship between Residual Entropy and entanglement across scales, as well as implications for space emergence from the RG flow of entangled field theories.

This study presents a family denoted as $SL^{n,m}$, applicable in any dimension, consisting of cohomologically rigid solvable Lie superalgebras with nilradical patterned after the filiform Lie superalgebra $L^{n,m$. Additionally, we introduce a collection of cohomologically rigid solvable Lie superalgebras with nilradical modeled after the generic characteristic sequence nilpotent Lie superalgebra. These instances represent solvable Lie superalgebras of maximum dimension associated with a specific nilradical. Conversely, it will be demonstrated that the family of Lie superalgebras $SL^{n,m}$ can undergo deformation when defined over a field with odd characteristics.

The presence of vector-like quarks (VLQs) is anticipated in various theoretical frameworks extending beyond the Standard Model (SM). In this study, we examine the potential for identifying the vector-like bottom quark (VLQ-$B$), characterized as an $SU(2)$ singlet with an electric charge of $-1/3$, at the Large Hadron Electron Collider (LHeC) within a model-independent context. We investigate the decay characteristics and individual production mechanisms of VLQ-$B$ at the LHeC, exploring three distinct signature types. Through a swift simulation encompassing both signal and background scenarios, we derive the signal significances. Our numerical findings suggest that detecting VLQ-$B$ through the semileptonic channel is more efficacious compared to the fully hadronic or leptonic channels.

The pharmacopeia utilized by medical practitioners and the general populace during the medieval period in Europe has often been disregarded as mere placebos or superstitions. Although it is now acknowledged that certain medicinal substances used by medieval healers may have possessed beneficial biological properties, the study of this subject is hindered by the arduous process of examining and interpreting ancient medical manuscripts. In this study, we showcase the potential effectiveness of transforming medieval medical writings into contextual electronic databases that can be analyzed using algorithms. By applying established methodologies from network science, we uncover significant statistical trends in the selection and utilization of ingredients in a pivotal text, the fifteenth-century Lylye of Medicynes, particularly focusing on treatments for symptoms related to microbial infections. We deliberate on the possibility that these trends indicate logical medical choices. Through presenting a detailed case study of data-driven textual analysis, we illustrate the promise of this approach in fostering interdisciplinary cooperation and shedding new light on the ethnopharmacology found within historical medical literature.

Attosecond streaking of atomic photoemission has the potential to offer groundbreaking insights into the timing of photoelectron release. Our research indicates that attosecond streaking phase shifts do indeed contain timing information related to the Eisenbud-Wigner-Smith time delay matrix of quantum scattering. However, accessing this information requires accurate consideration of the impact of the streaking infrared (IR) field on the emission process. The IR probe field can significantly alter the observed streaking phase shift. We demonstrate that the portion of the phase shift (time shift) resulting from the interaction between the outgoing electron and the combined Coulomb and IR laser fields can be explained using classical methods. In contrast, uncovering the strong initial-state dependence of the streaking phase shift necessitates solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation in its entirety. Our findings reveal a time delay exceeding 20 attoseconds between the hydrogenic 2s and 2p initial states in He+ across a broad spectrum of IR intensities and XUV energies.

The radial movement and dispersion of dust particles in protoplanetary disks impact the opacity, temperature, and timing of planetesimal formation. This study presents results from numerical simulations of particle-gas interactions in protoplanetary disks with varying dust grain sizes. Three scenarios are considered based on the Stokes number ($\tau_{\rm{s}}$) ranges: $10^{-1} - 10^0$, $10^{-4} - 10^{-1}$, and $10^{-3} - 10^{0}$. Both discrete and continuous size distributions of particles are examined. Our multi-species simulations reveal that different particle sizes interact with the gas, altering their dynamics compared to single-species scenarios. Larger particles induce streaming instability, generating turbulence that facilitates solid material diffusion. The radial equilibrium velocity shows reduced radial drift for large particles in multi-species simulations, while smaller particles tend to move outward on average. By adjusting the steepness of the size distribution (represented by the exponent $q$ in the solid number density distribution equation $dN/da \propto a^{-q}$), with values of $q = 3$ or $q = 4, we observe that small grains are lifted above the sedimented midplane layer where larger particles are concentrated. The measured diffusion and drift parameters obtained can inform coagulation models for planet formation and provide insights into the mixing processes of primitive meteorite components (matrix, chondrules, and CAIs) before their incorporation into parent bodies.

We have identified LP 400-22 (WD 2234+222) as a high-velocity white dwarf with very low mass. Analysis of ultraviolet GALEX and optical photometric colors, along with spectral line analysis, reveals that this star has an effective temperature of 11080+/-140 K and a surface gravity of log g = 6.32+/-0.08. As such, it is classified as a helium core white dwarf with a mass of 0.17 M_solar. With a tangential velocity of 414+/-43 km/s, LP 400-22 is among the fastest moving white dwarfs known. We will now explore potential evolutionary pathways for this remarkable celestial object.

Building upon our prior research [1], we delve into the task of discerning the splitting of the normal bundle of rational curves. Through the application of apolarity theory, we can identify specific subvarieties within certain Hilbert schemes of rational curves. These subvarieties are defined by the type of splitting exhibited by the normal bundle and the constrained tangent bundle.

We present two ground-based observing campaigns focused on establishing a grid of around 200 spectrophotometric standard stars (SPSS) with an internal precision of approximately 1% and calibrated to Vega within about 3%. This grid is essential for the absolute flux calibration of data collected by Gaia, the ESA astrometric mission. The selection criteria and a candidate list are provided, along with details on the survey strategy and data analysis methods employed. Additionally, we address a few challenging cases of rejected SPSS candidates, attributed to issues such as identification discrepancies, conflicting literature data, visual companions, and variability. Notably, all candidates undergo monitoring for constancy (within approximately 5 mmag). Specifically, we observed that the CALSPEC standard 1740346 exhibited delta Scuti variability during our short-term monitoring campaign lasting 1-2 hours.

Driven by advancements in robust optimization theory and the application of reinforcement learning, robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) have garnered increasing interest for their ability to make sequential decisions in uncertain environments. This review offers a comprehensive examination of the evolution and progress in RMDP formulations, specifically focusing on ambiguity modeling. It categorizes methods for representing uncertainty into three main approaches: parametric, moment-based, and discrepancy-based, while discussing the trade-offs involved in each representation.

Furthermore, the review explores the assumptions underlying the tractability of RMDPs, known for their conservative nature. It outlines three common rectangular conditions and introduces a new proof demonstrating the NP-hardness of non-rectangular RMDPs. Beyond the traditional scope of RMDPs, recent research efforts that challenge conventional rectangular assumptions and introduce new trends within the RMDP community are also analyzed. These studies contribute to the development of more adaptable and practical modeling frameworks, ultimately enhancing the performance and flexibility of RMDPs.

At high energies, the primary mechanism for the production of $c\bar{c}$ pairs is gluon-gluon fusion. Previously, this process has been studied using NLO collinear and k$_t$-factorization approaches. However, the current understanding of gluon distributions does not provide precise predictions for $c\bar{c}$ production at the LHC, especially at forward rapidities. This study explores $c\bar{c}$ pair production incorporating additional subleading mechanisms such as $gg \to Q\bar{Q}$, $\gamma g \to Q\bar{Q}$, $g\gamma \to Q\bar{Q}$, and $\gamma \gamma \to Q\bar{Q}$. The analysis utilizes MRST-QED parton distributions that account for photons as partons in protons, along with elastic photon distributions calculated using the equivalent photon approximation. The study presents distributions of $c$ quark ($\bar{c}$ antiquark) rapidity and transverse momenta, comparing them to the dominant gluon-gluon fusion contribution. Furthermore, inclusive single and central diffractive processes are discussed, incorporating diffractive parton distributions derived from HERA diffractive data analysis. Similar to the previous analysis, distributions in $c$ ($\bar{c}$) rapidity and transverse momentum are presented. Lastly, results for an exclusive central diffractive mechanism recently addressed in literature are presented, alongside corresponding differential distributions compared to single and central diffractive components.

Quantum steering, a key quantum resource for various quantum information processing tasks like quantum key distribution and true randomness generation, falls between entanglement and nonlocality. Detecting and measuring quantum steering is essential for these applications. Semi-definite programming (SDP) is a useful tool for quantifying quantum steering, but identifying the optimal measurement strategy can be time-consuming. Additionally, SDP requires full information of the quantum state, necessitating complex quantum state tomography.

In this study, we employ a semi-supervised self-training model to estimate the steerable weight, a crucial measure of quantum steering. This model can be trained with limited labeled data, reducing the labeling time. By constructing features based on probabilities from three sets of projective measurements under local unitary transformations on target states, we eliminate the need for quantum tomography. The model demonstrates strong generalization abilities and achieves high precision with minimal resources.

The software algorithms developed for the CMS tracker are described, focusing on reconstructing charged-particle trajectories in proton-proton interactions. These algorithms also estimate the positions of the LHC luminous region and individual primary-interaction vertices. Despite the challenging environment at the LHC, these algorithms demonstrate excellent performance. 

For ttbar events under typical 2011 pileup conditions, the average track-reconstruction efficiency for promptly-produced charged particles with transverse momenta greater than 0.9 GeV is 94% for pseudorapidities less than 0.9, and 85% for pseudorapidities between 0.9 and 2.5. The inefficiency primarily arises from hadrons undergoing nuclear interactions in the tracker material. However, for isolated muons, efficiencies are nearly perfect at 100%. 

In the case of isolated muons with a transverse momentum of 100 GeV emitted at pseudorapidities less than 1.4, resolutions are approximately 2.8% in transverse momentum, and around 10 microns and 30 microns in transverse and longitudinal impact parameters respectively. The position resolution achieved for reconstructed primary vertices corresponding to significant pp collisions is about 10-12 microns in each spatial dimension.

The tracking and vertexing software are characterized by speed and flexibility, easily adaptable for various functions like fast tracking for triggers or dedicated tracking for electrons considering bremsstrahlung effects.

In smooth and convex multiobjective optimization problems, the Pareto optima set is diffeomorphic to a simplex of dimension $m-1$, where $m$ represents the number of objective functions. The vertices of this simplex correspond to the optima of individual functions, while the $(k-1)$-dimensional facets represent the Pareto optimal set of subproblems involving $k$ functions. This hierarchy of submanifolds forms a geometrical structure known as stratification. The combination of these manifolds, specifically the set of Pareto optima, is referred to as a stratified set. This discussion delves into how these geometrical structures extend to non-convex cases, reviews existing findings, and proposes potential recommendations for designing specialized optimization strategies.

In recent years, large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT have played a significant role in advancing various artificial intelligence applications, including natural language processing and software engineering. An area with potential but not fully explored is the use of LLMs in software testing, particularly in black-box testing. This study compares the test cases generated by ChatGPT with those created by human participants. ChatGPT (GPT-4) and four participants each developed black-box test cases for three applications based on specifications provided by the authors. The aim was to assess the practicality of the test cases, identify any shortcomings, and explore how ChatGPT could improve human testing strategies. Results show that ChatGPT can produce test cases that are generally comparable or slightly better than those created by humans in terms of test viewpoint coverage. Furthermore, our experiments revealed that when ChatGPT collaborates with humans, they are able to cover a significantly broader range of test viewpoints compared to working individually, indicating that a combination of human and ChatGPT input may be more effective than human pairs working together. However, it was noted that the test cases generated by ChatGPT have some issues that need to be addressed before implementation.

In a prior study by the primary authors, they introduced a non-holonomic model that extends micromorphic models and allows for curvature (disclinations) to emerge from kinematic values. In this current paper, a broadening of the classical Euler-Bernoulli and Timoshenko bending beam models based on the aforementioned work is suggested. The former model remains based on a single unidimensional scalar field, while the latter incorporates a third unidimensional scalar field to refine the second-order terms. It is demonstrated that the generalized Euler-Bernoulli beam displays curvature (disclinations) associated with a third-order derivative of displacement but lacks torsion (dislocations). Simultaneously, the generalized Timoshenko beam is shown to exhibit both curvature and torsion, with curvature linked to the non-holonomy introduced in the generalization. Ultimately, through variational calculus, approximate values for curvature in static equilibrium are derived when the second-order contribution becomes insignificant, along with an equation for torsion in the generalized Timoshenko beam.

We examine a Sklyanin algebra S with three generators, forming a quadratic algebra over field k with generators x, y, and z subject to the relations pxy + qyx + rzz = 0, pyz + qzy + rxx = 0, and pzx + qxz + ryy = 0, where p, q, and r are parameters from field k. This class of algebras has garnered significant attention, notably from Feigin & Odesskii and Artin, Tate & Van den Berg in the realm of algebraic geometry. They demonstrated that if at least two of the parameters p, q, and r are non-zero, and at least two of the numbers p^3, q^3, and r^3 are distinct, then S is Koszul and shares the same Hilbert series as the algebra of commutative polynomials in three variables. It has been widely acknowledged that achieving this objective purely through algebraic and combinatorial methods such as the Groebner basis technique is deemed unattainable. This paper aims to explore the combinatorial significance of Sklyanin algebras' properties like Koszulity, PBW, PHS, and Calabi-Yau. Additionally, it offers a novel constructive proof of the aforementioned results by Artin, Tate, and Van den Bergh. Furthermore, we delve into a broader category of Sklyanin algebras known as generalized Sklyanin algebras. This category encompasses scenarios where all parameters in the relations differ. We provide a classification of generalized Sklyanin algebras with polynomial Hilbert series up to isomorphism. It is shown that generalized Sklyanin algebras in general position exhibit the Golod-Shafarevich Hilbert series (except in cases involving fields with two elements).

This paper examines the observational characteristics of three common small-scale energetic events in the solar transition region (TR): TR explosive events, ultraviolet bursts, and jets. These events are identified through spectral and imaging data. Recent advancements in instrumentation have enabled researchers to gain valuable insights into these phenomena. These events serve as a useful tool for investigating the transfer of mass and energy between the solar chromosphere and corona. Given that the underlying physical mechanisms of these small-scale events may be akin to those governing larger-scale phenomena such as flares and coronal mass ejections, analyzing these events can enhance our comprehension of the solar atmosphere across varying scales. The observations of these small-scale energetic events underscore the dynamic nature of the TR, underscoring its significance as a critical layer in the solar atmosphere bridging the chromosphere and corona.

Wearable egocentric cameras combined with machine learning offer clinicians a more detailed insight into how patients use their hands at home following a stroke or spinal cord injury. To effectively interpret metrics and guide therapy planning, these technologies rely on comprehensive contextual information, including activities and interactions with objects. Our study demonstrates that by focusing on the objects patients interact with rather than their movements, an object-centric approach can accurately identify Activities of Daily Living (ADL) in real-world rehabilitation settings. We tested our models on a diverse dataset collected in natural environments, which included 2261 minutes of egocentric video footage from 16 participants with hand impairment. By utilizing pre-trained models for object detection and hand-object interactions, our system consistently performed well across different levels of impairment and environments. The best model achieved an impressive mean weighted F1-score of 0.78 +/- 0.12, maintaining an F1-score > 0.5 for all participants using leave-one-subject-out cross validation. Our qualitative analysis revealed that this approach provides clinically relevant information about functional object use while remaining resilient to variations in patient movements, making it ideal for rehabilitation settings where upper limb impairment is common.

Our analysis demonstrates a crucial link between the presence of the delta-function singularity within the chirally-odd twist-3 distribution $e(x)$ of the nucleon, and the persistent existence of the quark condensate as an indicator of the spontaneous chiral symmetry breakdown in the QCD vacuum. This singularity in $e(x)$, evident through a significant deviation from the 1st moment sum rule, represents a unique scenario where the intricate vacuum dynamics of QCD materialize in an observable associated with a localized QCD excitation, specifically, the nucleon.

Functional data analysis has undergone extensive research. This study focuses on a partially functional model where some covariates are scalars with linear effects, and others are functional with unspecified nonlinear effects. A significant improvement from previous studies is the consideration of interactions between functional and scalar covariates. To address long-tailed error distributions common in data analysis, the quantile technique is utilized for estimation. For more interpretable results and applicability in various settings, it is assumed that the effects of functional covariates are locally sparse, leading to a variable/model selection challenge. The proposed approach follows a main effect, interaction hierarchy, suggesting that if a subregion has a nonzero effect in an interaction term, its effect must also be nonzero in the corresponding main functional effect. A penalization method is introduced for estimation, identifying local sparsity, and adhering to the hierarchy. An efficient computational algorithm is devised, with consistency properties rigorously proven under mild conditions. Simulation results confirm the practical effectiveness of the proposed approach, while the analysis of Tecator data showcases its real-world applicability. In conclusion, this study introduces a novel and practically useful model along with a statistically and numerically sound estimation technique.

In real-time strategy (RTS) games, managing the complexity of artificial intelligence (AI) often involves using action and/or state abstractions. While high-level abstractions can enhance strategic decision-making, they may compromise tactical decision quality by omitting important details. On the other hand, sampling the search space can boost tactical performance in simple scenarios but may result in subpar high-level planning.

Our proposed approach combines the use of a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to choose from a limited set of abstract actions with game tree search to enhance low-level tactics. The CNN is trained through supervised learning on game states labeled by Puppet Search, an algorithm that employs action abstractions. This network then selects a script, or abstract action, to guide the actions of all units, while the game tree search algorithm refines the tactics of a subset of units based on a partial view of the game state focused on units near opponent units.

Experiments conducted in the microRTS game demonstrate that this integrated algorithm achieves higher win rates compared to its individual components and other advanced microRTS agents. Notably, this represents the first successful utilization of a convolutional network to play a complete RTS game on standard maps, as prior research has mainly concentrated on specific aspects like combat or small-scale maps.

The expansion of Large Language Models' (LLMs) capabilities through the incorporation of external tools has given rise to a promising field known as tool learning. While current studies on tool learning primarily concentrate on enhancing general-purpose tool-use skills to meet explicit user requirements, they tend to neglect the significance of personalized tool-use abilities, resulting in an inability to cater to implicit user preferences. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of personalized tool learning, which involves incorporating a user's interaction history to tailor tool usage to individual preferences. In response to the lack of suitable benchmarks, we have developed PEToolBench, a comprehensive platform that encompasses various user preferences derived from interaction histories across three distinct personalized settings, covering a wide array of tool-use scenarios. Additionally, we have proposed a framework called PEToolLLaMA aimed at adapting LLMs to personalized tool learning tasks, utilizing supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization during training. Extensive experiments conducted on PEToolBench demonstrate the superior performance of PEToolLLaMA compared to existing LLMs.

Renewable energy sources and increased electrification of energy consumption play a crucial role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions, while also adding complexity to the electric power system. The integration of automation, information and communication technology, and intelligent solutions has led to the evolution of the power system into a smart grid. To facilitate the advancement of smart grid solutions at a system level, comprehensive testing must be conducted to address the multi-domain nature of these intricate systems. This paper presents the concept of holistic power system testing and outlines initial steps towards developing a corresponding methodology within the European ERIGrid research infrastructure project.

We introduce a novel method for parton-to-hadron fragmentation within proton-proton collisions. Our approach involves considering the hadronization process in the parton-parton center-of-mass system, where hadrons are emitted in alignment with the outgoing partons before transforming their four-momenta into the overall center-of-mass system using appropriate Lorentz transformations. In cases of heavy hadron production, strict adherence to energy-momentum conditions is enforced. Notably, our methodology diverges from the commonly accepted notion that the rapidity of the produced hadron matches that of the parent parton.

To exemplify this innovative framework, we apply it to the production of $D$ mesons, $ Lambda_c$ baryons, and $ eta_c$ quarkonium within a leading-order parton production scenario. We present distributions for transverse momentum, rapidity, and Feynman-$x_F$, showcasing the distinctiveness of our approach. Specifically, we analyze processes such as $c  to D$, $g  to D$, $c  to  eta_c$, and $g  to  eta_c$ for hadronization.

The resulting rapidity distributions exhibit significantly reduced widths compared to traditional methods that assume rapidity equivalence between partons and hadrons. This has implications for both mid- and forward rapidities, potentially impacting high-energy neutrino production in Earth's atmosphere. Additionally, our examination of $c  to  Lambda_c^+$ and $b  to  Lambda_c^+$ fragmentation suggests that the latter mechanism may play a role in the heightened production of $ Lambda_c^{ pm}$ as recently observed by the ALICE collaboration.

Effective and comprehensive tool manipulation necessitates a deep understanding of the characteristics and capabilities of different tools. Our study explores the potential impact of linguistic details pertaining to a tool, such as its shape and typical functions, on the adaptability of control policies to new tools for specific tasks. By leveraging a variety of natural language descriptions for assorted tools, we utilize pre-existing language models to generate distinctive feature representations. Subsequently, through language-influenced meta-learning, we acquire knowledge on policies capable of swiftly adjusting to unfamiliar tools based on their corresponding textual descriptions. Our findings highlight the significant enhancement in tool acquisition speed across various manipulation tasks like pushing, lifting, sweeping, and hammering by integrating linguistic data with meta-learning techniques.

The analysis of two-level systems in time-varying backgrounds is currently being explored. New precise solutions are introduced for specific backgrounds that diminish over time. Additionally, inspired by the concepts proposed by Feynman, Vernon, and Hellwarth, we delve into the potential for simplifying quantum dynamics into a classical Hamiltonian system. This approach allows for the direct application of robust classical mechanics techniques, such as KAM methods, to analyze the quantum system. By adopting this methodology, we are able to make significant inferences regarding "quantum chaos" in scenarios where the external background exhibits periodic or quasi-periodic behavior over time.

An exact solution to the equations of motion for a two-field cosmological model, demonstrating multi-field dark energy, has been discovered. This dark energy is characterized by field-space trajectories featuring consistently high turning rates. Our analysis focuses on a specific class of two-field models, revealing the feasibility of these trajectories leading to accelerated expansion of space-time, even when the scalar potential maintains the rotational invariance of the field-space metric. In the context of Poincaré-disk field space, we have determined the scalar potential form that aligns with these background solutions and have successfully obtained exact analytical solutions. These solutions exhibit field-space trajectories spiraling inward towards the center of the Poincaré disk. Notably, the functional form of the relevant scalar potential exhibits compatibility with a particular hidden symmetry, despite being disrupted by the presence of a constant term.

Mechanical issues in real-world scenarios can lead to deviations in observation values, resulting in anomalies in multivariate time series like sensor readings or network data. Understanding the temporal context and interrelationships among variables is crucial for detecting these anomalies effectively. Detecting anomalies in time series data, especially when dealing with unlabeled data, is a complex task. To tackle this challenge, we propose a self-supervised model training approach that involves using a data degradation scheme. This scheme involves introducing synthetic outliers into the data by replacing a portion of the input with these outliers. By leveraging the self-attention mechanism, we have developed a Transformer-based architecture that can efficiently recognize temporal patterns and identify abnormal sequences. Our model transforms multivariate data points into temporal representations with relative position bias, generating anomaly scores based on these representations. Known as AnomalyBERT, our method demonstrates superior performance in detecting anomalies within intricate time series data, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques across five real-world benchmarks. For access to our code, visit https://github.com/Jhryu30/AnomalyBERT.

The growing need for controllable outputs in text-to-image generation has driven progress in multi-instance generation (MIG), enabling users to specify both instance layouts and attributes. However, unlike image-conditional generation approaches like ControlNet, MIG techniques have not been widely integrated into cutting-edge models such as SD2 and SDXL. This is mainly due to the complexity of developing robust renderers that can handle instance positioning and attribute rendering simultaneously. 

In this study, we present Depth-Driven Decoupled Instance Synthesis (3DIS), a new framework that breaks down the MIG process into two stages: first, creating a coarse scene depth map for precise instance positioning and scene composition, and then rendering detailed attributes using a pre-trained ControlNet on any base model without the need for additional training. Our 3DIS framework incorporates a tailored adapter into LDM3D for accurate depth-based layouts and utilizes a fine-tuning-free approach for improved instance-level attribute rendering.

Extensive experiments conducted on the COCO-Position and COCO-MIG benchmarks demonstrate that 3DIS surpasses existing methods in both layout accuracy and attribute rendering quality. Importantly, 3DIS seamlessly integrates with various base models, offering a reliable and adaptable solution for advanced multi-instance generation tasks. The code for 3DIS can be accessed at: https://github.com/limuloo/3DIS.
